details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A simple pattern may not handle open-ended troubleshooting, but it is easier to evaluate and operate for this bounded use case.
details.errorCorrection: Start with the augmented LLM building block when retrieval, tools, or memory are enough and no dynamic process is required.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The handbook is an external knowledge augmentation; the answer cites the selected passage and can abstain when the source does not support it.
details.scenarioApplication: The manufacturer can update the handbook index without creating an agent loop for a question-answering task.
details.transfer: Use this pattern for manuals, FAQs, and stable internal knowledge where the response is the product and the source boundary is clear.

messages.text: The retrieval tool is useful, but exploratory agentic planning adds autonomy and a loop when the handbook already supports a bounded grounded response.
Classification and a second stage can be valid at larger scale, but the extra routing path adds latency without a stated category or ambiguity problem.
Separate research and writing agents duplicate the same source context and coordination work for a single evidence-grounded answer.

feedback.reason: Retrieval or supplied context augments a single LLM response and directly serves the grounded question. More autonomy would add complexity without a decision or action to coordinate.

options.text: An augmented LLM that receives or retrieves the handbook context and answers with a citation.
An agent with a read-only handbook retrieval tool that may explore follow-up questions before citing an answer.
A routing workflow that first classifies the question, then retrieves handbook context and renders a cited answer.
Two coordinated agents, one researching the handbook and one writing the answer, both reading the same source before responding.

questions.prompt: A small manufacturer has a 60-page, authoritative maintenance handbook. Technicians ask questions that can be answered from the handbook, and the application should cite the relevant passage. There is no need to take actions or plan multiple steps. Which pattern is the best fit?

constraints: The number and order of searches cannot be known before the investigation.
New evidence changes the next action.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Adaptive exploration can discover relevant evidence but has less predictable cost and latency, so explicit limits and review are part of the design.
details.errorCorrection: Diagnose whether uncertainty is about the next step itself; if it is, replace a rigid sequence with an evaluated, bounded loop rather than simply adding more fixed calls.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The agent observes intermediate findings, selects a next tool call, and writes checkpoints; limits on steps, time, and spend prevent an unbounded loop.
details.scenarioApplication: The research agent should record queries and sources, pursue newly relevant leads, and stop when coverage or budget criteria are met for lead review.
details.transfer: Use agentic control for open-ended investigation, planning, or discovery only when its adaptive benefit can be measured against a bounded stop condition.

messages.text: A fixed three-call limit cannot adapt when evidence requires a different number or order of searches.
Manual follow-up leaves the system unable to execute the evidence-dependent work and does not diagnose the pattern mismatch.
Searching every possibility wastes budget and still cannot decide which follow-up matters after a discovery.

feedback.reason: The next action is evidence-dependent, so a fixed chain cannot represent the work. A bounded agent can adapt while budgets, source records, and a stopping rule keep exploration operationally safe.

options.text: Encode a fixed sequence of three search calls and truncate any investigation that needs a fourth.
Use a static retrieval prompt and let the analyst manually perform every follow-up search outside the system.
Run all possible searches in parallel before seeing evidence, then concatenate the results for Claude.
Use a bounded agentic loop that chooses the next search from evidence, records sources, and stops on explicit budget or sufficiency criteria.

questions.prompt: A market-research assistant faces an unpredictable number of searches and follow-up paths; each discovery can change the next question. Which pattern addresses the actual failure of a fixed workflow?

constraints: The common 80% has a stable, bounded path.
The 20% needs adaptive discovery and its own budget and review boundary.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Two paths add routing and maintenance overhead, but they avoid paying agentic cost on routine work while retaining discovery where it creates value.
details.errorCorrection: Do not let a minority of open-ended cases force all traffic through an agent or let a stable path hide missing evidence.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A classifier or explicit request type selects the augmented workflow or bounded agent; each path has its own evaluation, permissions, and stop conditions.
details.scenarioApplication: Measure FAQ accuracy and latency separately from investigation coverage, source quality, and budget, and send uncertain routing or agent completion to review.
details.transfer: Segment workloads by whether the next action is predictable and then evaluate a workflow and an agentic path against their actual slices.

messages.text: Universal agentic execution spends exploratory cost on routine questions and makes the stable workload less predictable.
The fixed knowledge base cannot supply evidence for the investigation slice and would produce confident incompleteness.
Answer length is not a quality or evidence criterion, and duplicate execution doubles cost without a route decision.

feedback.reason: The workload has two distinct decision structures: most cases have a known retrieval-and-answer path, while a minority benefits from adaptive search. Routing keeps each pattern proportionate.

options.text: Route stable questions through an augmented workflow and send investigation cases to a bounded agentic path with explicit stop and review criteria.
Use the agentic path for every question so the system has one architecture and can discover new sources when needed.
Use the fixed knowledge base for every question and return its best passage when investigation evidence is missing.
Run both paths for every request and select the longer answer as the more complete result.

questions.prompt: A support service handles 80% of questions with a stable knowledge base and fixed answer format. The remaining 20% require investigation across changing sources and follow-up searches. Which architecture should route the two workloads?

constraints: Normal intake steps and output schema are fixed.
Only the exception branch needs adaptive evidence search; the final policy check is deterministic.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The hybrid design requires explicit branching and monitoring, but it avoids unnecessary agent cost and protects the release gate.
details.errorCorrection: Place adaptive behavior at the smallest branch that requires discovery, while retaining deterministic gates around the external decision.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The workflow produces a typed intake and a flag; the agent searches relevant evidence under limits, and ordinary code enforces the final policy contract.
details.scenarioApplication: Process routine records through fixed stages, route flagged exceptions with their context and budget, and quarantine any record failing the final check.
details.transfer: When only exceptions are open-ended, use a predictable workflow as the spine and isolate adaptive search behind a measured, bounded branch.

messages.text: Applying exploration to every intake ignores the fixed normal path and raises cost and variability without evidence.
Manual exception work loses the opportunity for a controlled adaptive branch and leaves the state unobservable.
A citation can be stale or inapplicable; it does not replace the deterministic policy check.

feedback.reason: The normal path is known and the exception path is evidence-dependent. A workflow plus a bounded subpath preserves deterministic validation while granting exploration only where needed.

options.text: Send every intake through an open-ended agent so routine records and exceptions share one adaptive path.
Use one fixed prompt and have analysts investigate exceptions manually without recording an exception state.
Implement a workflow for extraction and validation, invoke a bounded agent only on flagged exceptions, then run the policy check before release.
Skip the policy check when the exception agent returns a cited passage because citation presence proves compliance.

questions.prompt: A compliance intake has a fixed extraction, validation, and schema sequence. Only exceptions require searching a changing evidence store, and all final records pass a deterministic policy check. Which architecture is most appropriate?

constraints: The next read tool and number of checks depend on live equipment readings.
Inspection tools are read-only, but the proposed repair is consequential.
Safety thresholds, deterministic checks, and human approval must stop the action path.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If every answer came only from the handbook and no live tool or action were needed, retain the augmented LLM boundary in CCARP-D01-O03-boundary.
details.errorCorrection: Static handbook context cannot execute or adapt to live evidence, and inference from absent readings can produce an unsafe repair recommendation.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic says agents fit open-ended problems whose number of steps cannot be predicted and describes them as LLMs using tools in a loop. The scenario's mechanism is governed by this decisive constraint: The action path has evidence-dependent steps and a consequential approval boundary, unlike a one-shot cited handbook answer.
details.scenarioApplication: Use a bounded agentic loop for read-only inspection with explicit stop conditions, then pass the proposed repair and evidence through deterministic checks and human approval before action.
details.transfer: Use measured evidence and the stated authority boundary to choose the least complex design that satisfies the workload's constraint; revisit the route when the counterfactual changes.

messages.text: Static handbook context cannot execute or adapt to live evidence, and inference from absent readings can produce an unsafe repair recommendation.
A single unrestricted call has no explicit stop conditions or enforceable approval boundary for the consequential repair.
This avoids the adaptive inspection the scenario requires and escalates routine evidence gathering instead of using bounded read-only checks.

feedback.reason: The required pattern changes when the system must choose follow-up tools from new evidence; the action boundary remains outside unrestricted model control.

options.text: Use a bounded read-only agent loop, then require deterministic checks and human approval before repair.
Use the augmented LLM handbook path and ask the technician to infer the live reading and next action from the answer.
Expose all read and repair tools in one call and let the model choose the repair action whenever readings suggest it.
Use a fixed checklist and escalate every case to a technician without inspecting live readings through tools.

questions.prompt:
Technicians ask a maintenance question from a handbook and may then inspect live equipment, select among read tools based on readings, stop at a safety threshold, and request approval before a repair action.

Which interaction pattern fits the evidence-dependent inspection and repair boundary?

constraints: An exact lookup resolves 94% of requests at 220 ms p95 under a 500 ms synchronous SLA.
Only no-match or conflicting records create the evidence gap; research is five times more expensive.
Research has a separate three-minute asynchronous contract with pending and human escalation states.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the exact lookup never produced a no-match or conflict, remove the asynchronous research job; if the business accepted one three-minute response for every request, re-evaluate the synchronous routing boundary.
details.errorCorrection: The evidence gap is known only after the exact lookup, and inline research would violate the routine 500 ms contract when the catalog can resolve the request.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Just-in-time retrieval uses lightweight identifiers to load detailed information only when relevant, keeping context focused. The scenario's mechanism is governed by this decisive constraint: Keep the 500 ms synchronous contract for routine exact lookups and defer the expensive research branch to an explicit asynchronous path only after the lookup proves an evidence gap.
details.scenarioApplication: Run the exact structured lookup synchronously, return its grounded result when it succeeds, and enqueue a bounded agentic research job only on a no-match or conflict state; expose pending, completion, citations, cost, and the three-minute timeout rather than running research inline.
details.transfer: Use measured evidence and the stated authority boundary to choose the least complex design that satisfies the workload's constraint; revisit the route when the counterfactual changes.

messages.text: The evidence gap is known only after the exact lookup, and inline research would violate the routine 500 ms contract when the catalog can resolve the request.
Always researching wastes the cheap deterministic path and turns 94% of requests into unnecessary asynchronous work.
A no-match is the trigger for bounded research or human handling; a provisional semantic result does not satisfy the grounded-answer and evidence-state contract.

feedback.reason: The routing decision is between a fast synchronous first stage and a deferred evidence-gap job with its own SLA, not a generic choice to make every hard request agentic.

options.text: Classify the user message as routine or investigative before lookup and run the research loop inline for messages that appear complex.
Perform the exact lookup synchronously; research asynchronously only after a no-match or conflict, with explicit pending and timeout states.
Always enqueue the three-minute research job, even when the exact lookup succeeds, so every response has the same evidence depth.
Return the top semantic result immediately when the exact lookup has no match and mark its citation as provisional.

questions.prompt:
A product-support workflow first performs an exact SKU and warranty-status lookup. For 94% of requests it returns a grounded answer in 220 ms p95 under a 500 ms synchronous SLA; for 6% it returns no active match or conflicting records. A research pilot improves accepted resolution on that evidence-gap slice from 61% to 79% but costs five times as much.

Which routing design preserves the synchronous contract while using research where it adds value?

constraints: The subtasks and their order are known in advance.
A deterministic style gate must run before publication.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Explicit stages require orchestration code and intermediate storage, but they provide reproducible gates and clearer failure localization.
details.errorCorrection: Choose a workflow when the path is predictable; reserve agentic loops for cases where the next action genuinely depends on discovery.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Each Claude call performs one bounded transformation, and the application controls the sequence and style validator between calls.
details.scenarioApplication: Research output feeds the draft call, the draft feeds the style check, and a failed check returns a structured revision request rather than publication.
details.transfer: Map known business steps and mandatory gates before selecting an architecture; the pattern should follow process uncertainty, not novelty.

messages.text: Autonomous planning adds variability and cost without addressing a missing step in this fixed process.
One response hides stage failures and gives no independent style gate before publication.
Routing chooses among paths but does not represent the required order or enforce the fixed validation gate.

feedback.reason: Known subtasks and ordering favor a workflow whose stages and gate are explicit. Prompt chaining makes each handoff testable and avoids paying for unneeded autonomous planning.

options.text: Use an open-ended agent that chooses its own research and revision loop even though every required step and gate is already known.
Use a prompt-chained workflow with explicit research, drafting, and style-validation steps, passing structured output between them.
Use a single unrestricted prompt that asks Claude to research, draft, and self-approve the article in one response.
Use a routing layer that sends each article to whichever specialist appears most relevant, without encoding the fixed sequence.

questions.prompt: An editorial service must draft an article from a fixed outline, run a known sequence of research and drafting steps, and pass a fixed style gate before publication. Which architecture is the best fit?

constraints: Most messages map to stable categories and category-specific paths.
Ambiguous classification needs a human route rather than an invented action.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Routing is less flexible for novel requests and requires category maintenance, but it gives predictable permissions and a controlled human path.
details.errorCorrection: Use routing when known categories have distinct procedures; design uncertainty as a first-class branch rather than force a best guess.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A classifier selects a bounded category path; the route can carry uncertainty to a human or refuse execution rather than turn a low-confidence label into a side effect.
details.scenarioApplication: Delivery, damaged-item, and access messages each invoke their approved policy/API path, while unresolved classification enters a review queue with the evidence shown.
details.transfer: For operations with stable classes and materially different actions, separate classification, routing, and ambiguity handling before considering a free-form agent.

messages.text: Exploring all tools on every message spends cost and exposes unnecessary actions when the normal paths are already known.

A shared path does not enforce the distinct category policy and API contract before a side effect; deferring ambiguity to a post-action exception can send a sensitive or invalid request to the wrong route.
A description without a route leaves the operational work undone and does not enforce the category-specific policy.
Without category routing, the known policy/API paths cannot be selected consistently or evaluated as bounded workflows.
Without a pre-action ambiguity route, uncertain requests are forced into a category-specific operation instead of reaching a human safely.

feedback.reason: Stable categories justify a routing step, while ambiguity needs an explicit safe state at the route boundary. Together they prevent exploratory tool use and false certainty.

options.text: Let one agent explore every support tool for every message so it can discover the best category at runtime.
Classify the request, route it to the corresponding policy and API workflow, and use a confidence or ambiguity state for human handoff.
Apply one general support workflow and shared policy/API surface to every category, then send exceptions to a human after the workflow has attempted the request.
Use one fixed prompt for all categories and ask Claude to describe the next API call without executing a route.
Route ambiguous or low-confidence messages to a human queue with the evidence and candidate categories, without invoking a category-specific API.

questions.prompt: A support platform has stable delivery, damaged-item, and account-access categories, each with its own API and policy path. Ambiguous messages must reach a human. Which TWO design choices fit this workload? Select TWO.

constraints: The specialist scopes are separate but their evidence must support one conclusion.
Workers may research but cannot issue the customer-facing decision.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A lead stage adds elapsed time and a synthesis dependency, but it prevents inconsistent customer conclusions and supports an auditable handoff.
details.errorCorrection: Use specialization for research breadth without distributing final decision authority across unsynchronized agents.
details.mechanismOrProperty: An orchestrator delegates scoped research and collects artifacts; a lead checks provenance, resolves conflicts, and controls the final output.
details.scenarioApplication: Each worker cites applicable labor, tax, or environmental sources and states uncertainty; the lead checks the combined facts before drafting the customer response.
details.transfer: For multi-domain advice, put research authority with scoped workers and communication or decision authority with one validated owner.

messages.text: One worker combines unrelated rule sets and removes the independent evidence and specialization the scenario requires.
Allowing each specialist to answer the customer creates conflicting authority before any reconciliation.
An undifferentiated prompt provides no per-domain ownership or evidence contract and leaves interpretation unreviewed.

feedback.reason: The work naturally decomposes by rule set, but authority for the final conclusion belongs to the lead. Structured worker evidence makes that boundary explicit.

options.text: Ask one worker to research all three rule sets and publish its conclusion directly to the customer.
Give each specialist full authority to answer the customer and reconcile conflicting conclusions after delivery.
Run one undifferentiated prompt containing all rule sets and let Claude choose the most persuasive interpretation.
Assign bounded specialist workers with source and output contracts, then require a lead to validate evidence and synthesize the customer-facing conclusion.

questions.prompt: Labor, tax, and environmental specialists research separate rule sets and return evidence. Only a lead may issue the customer-facing conclusion. Which boundary should the architect implement?

constraints: The edits share dependencies and repository state.
Concurrent workers are causing conflicts rather than independent throughput.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Coordination reduces apparent concurrency and adds merge checkpoints, but it avoids repeated conflict repair and protects repository correctness.
details.errorCorrection: Diagnose contention and dependency structure before increasing concurrency; parallelism is useful only across independent work.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A dependency map and coordinator establish a partial order, while isolated branches or bounded parallel tasks reduce write conflicts before integration checks.
details.scenarioApplication: Sequence schema changes before dependent callers, run independent documentation edits in parallel, and require tests or compatibility checks at each merge point.
details.transfer: When agents modify shared artifacts, classify dependencies and ownership first; use parallelism inside an explicit integration plan.

messages.text: More workers amplify writes to the same dependent state and do not resolve the underlying ordering conflict.
Complete shared history and a final merge review do not coordinate dependent writes; the conflicting edits have already been created before that review.
Removing validation defers the conflict to the end and allows a broken repository to accumulate.

feedback.reason: The failure is not a lack of workers; it is shared mutable state and dependency ordering. The design must coordinate dependent edits and preserve validation barriers.

options.text: Map dependencies and assign a coordinator to sequence dependent edits, while parallelizing only changes proven independent and validating each integration point.
Increase the number of concurrent agents and ask each to resolve conflicts from the latest shared repository state.
Give every agent the complete repository history, allow dependent edits to proceed concurrently, and rely on one final merge review to reconcile conflicting assumptions.
Remove all validation gates so agents can commit quickly and reconcile the resulting repository at the end.

questions.prompt: Four migration agents receive shared repository history and edit dependent files concurrently. They overwrite assumptions, create conflicts, and require repeated reconciliation. What architectural diagnosis follows?

constraints: Market-level outputs must exist before their specialists run.
Workers need local evidence scopes and the lead owns global synthesis.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The hierarchy adds orchestration state and barriers, but it prevents cross-market contamination and makes failures attributable to a market or specialist.
details.errorCorrection: Use hierarchical orchestration when dependencies repeat at two levels; do not flatten a gated tree into global fanout.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A parent orchestrator creates child market workflows, each with scoped evidence and a local barrier, before a top-level lead aggregates the structured outputs.
details.scenarioApplication: Record market and worker IDs, enforce local source boundaries, require citations and uncertainty, and let the lead reconcile cross-market comparisons.
details.transfer: For nested research or processing, create explicit parent-child scope and readiness conditions before allowing lower-level concurrency.

messages.text: Full global context wastes budget and can contaminate each market with evidence from another market.
A single sequential context is slow and makes local evidence boundaries and intermediate failures hard to inspect.
Shared mutable notes create race conditions and postpone conflict handling until after an unauditable final report.

feedback.reason: The dependency is hierarchical: a market summary gates its local specialists, while specialist tasks can then run in parallel and the lead owns synthesis.

options.text: Launch every specialist for every market with the full global corpus, then ask the lead to infer market ownership from the reports.
Run one global agent sequentially through all markets and ask it to remember each local evidence set for final synthesis.
Use a hierarchical orchestrator: create market tasks, fan out scoped legal/pricing/competitor workers after each market summary, then send structured market reports to the lead.
Run all specialists in parallel against shared mutable notes and reconcile conflicting market facts after the report is delivered.

questions.prompt: A global diligence project first needs market summaries, then legal, pricing, and competitor specialists for each market. Specialist work is independent within a market, each worker must receive only its market evidence, and a lead must synthesize one report. Which design is best?

constraints: The two figures have different dated source filings.
The final report needs provenance and an explicit conflict resolution before publication.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Verification delays publication and may leave an explicit unknown, but it protects the report from a confident blended figure.
details.errorCorrection: When specialists disagree, create a bounded adjudication step instead of smoothing the values or trusting recency without checking scope.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A lead can spawn a targeted worker with the exact sources and question, then join its finding and confidence to the report before publication.
details.scenarioApplication: Compare reporting periods, units, and extraction spans, record the resolved interpretation or unresolved state, and expose both citations in the final report.
details.transfer: Use targeted conflict-resolution tasks with preserved source lineage whenever parallel workers produce incompatible material facts.

messages.text: Averaging figures from different periods can invent a value that no filing supports and hides the reason for disagreement.
Rewriting whole reports increases cost and does not verify the specific conflicting evidence.
Recency alone does not prove that the newer filing covers the same period or corrects the older extraction.

feedback.reason: A conflict between dated filings is an evidence-resolution task, not a prose or averaging task. The orchestrator should preserve provenance, narrow verification, and block synthesis until the discrepancy is explained.

options.text: Ask the lead to average the figures and cite both filings so the report contains one number.
Create a focused verification task for the conflicting filings, preserve both dated evidence paths, and let the lead publish only after the period or extraction issue is resolved.
Have every worker rewrite the entire report independently and select the version with the most consistent prose.
Drop the older filing because a newer document must supersede it even when the reporting periods may differ.

questions.prompt: A multi-agent diligence report contains conflicting revenue figures from two dated regulatory filings. The lead must decide whether the discrepancy is a genuine period difference or an extraction error before publishing. What should the orchestration do?

constraints: All twelve analysts need the full evolving context and later work depends on earlier interpretations.
Prior parallel runs produced contradictory state and reconciliation work.
A lead owns the final brief and needs an explicit checkpoint.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If each market had independent evidence and no worker depended on another's state, use the parallel specialist design from CCARP-D01-O04-selection.
details.errorCorrection: Shared context and dependent edits create conflicts before synthesis, so a final reconciliation cannot recover reliable ownership or ordering.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic notes that multi-agent systems are a poor fit when agents must share the same context or when many dependencies exist between agents. The scenario's mechanism is governed by this decisive constraint: The workers share context and have many dependencies, so independent parallel agents would not create isolated throughput.
details.scenarioApplication: Use one coordinated context with staged handoffs or a small dependency-aware workflow, preserving a lead checkpoint rather than fanning out twelve independent agents.
details.transfer: Use measured evidence and the stated authority boundary to choose the least complex design that satisfies the workload's constraint; revisit the route when the counterfactual changes.

messages.text: Shared context and dependent edits create conflicts before synthesis, so a final reconciliation cannot recover reliable ownership or ordering.
Isolation removes simultaneous writes but does not resolve the many dependencies; the lead still receives inconsistent states too late to control ordering.
A single serial worker avoids conflicts but discards useful specialist work and does not provide the bounded dependency-aware handoffs the scenario can support.

feedback.reason: Multi-agent parallelism is a poor fit when workers must share the same context and many dependencies; coordination should follow the actual topology.

options.text: Run twelve parallel specialists with full shared context and ask the lead to reconcile all differences at the end.
Give each specialist an isolated snapshot and ask the lead to merge all twelve reports after they finish.
Use coordinated staged handoffs with a lead checkpoint instead of independent shared-context fanout.
Have the lead perform every analysis serially in one context with no specialist handoffs or staged checkpoints.

questions.prompt:
Twelve analysts investigate one shared market model. Each analyst needs the full evolving context, and the next analyst's task depends on the previous analyst's interpretation; a lead still owns the final brief.

Which orchestration shape fits the shared context and dependency structure?

constraints: Five workers are complete; one worker's scope is revoked after retrieval and before synthesis.
Organization policy requires valid access at aggregation for every mandatory region.
An unavailable region may be published only when the policy explicitly marks that region optional.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If current scope remains valid at aggregation, accept the packet after the same source and completeness checks. If policy explicitly designates the region optional, publish the other regions with that region marked unavailable.
details.errorCorrection: The organization policy requires valid access at aggregation for the mandatory region, and neighboring evidence is not authority for that jurisdiction; inferred coverage would falsely claim completeness.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic found that workers need an objective, output format, tool and source guidance, and clear task boundaries to avoid duplicated work and gaps. The scenario's mechanism is governed by this decisive constraint: Parallelism remains useful, but the organization policy makes current authorization at aggregation an admissibility gate; retrieved data is not automatically invalidated by OAuth revocation, yet it cannot be published for a mandatory region without a current policy-approved access decision.
details.scenarioApplication: Run bounded scoped workers in parallel, revalidate current scope and policy at aggregation, quarantine the revoked worker packet, and reauthorize or retry it before synthesis. Do not publish the complete comparison; publish an explicit unavailable region only if the governing policy permits that region to be optional.
details.transfer: Use measured evidence and the stated authority boundary to choose the least complex design that satisfies the workload's constraint; revisit the route when the counterfactual changes.

messages.text: The organization policy requires valid access at aggregation for the mandatory region, and neighboring evidence is not authority for that jurisdiction.
A single revoked packet requires quarantine and reauthorization; discarding valid independent evidence creates unnecessary cost and delay without improving the policy decision.
A partial publication is allowed only when the governing policy makes the region optional; otherwise the complete comparison must stop until the mandatory evidence is admissible.

feedback.reason: The topology stays parallel while the organization policy, rather than revocation alone, determines whether an already retrieved packet may enter the lead’s synthesis.

options.text: Accept the five returned packets because the revoked worker already retrieved its evidence, and infer the mandatory jurisdiction from neighboring reports.
Discard all six packets and restart the entire investigation whenever any worker scope changes.
Publish the five-region comparison and label the mandatory region unavailable regardless of policy.
Run scoped workers, revalidate scope and policy at aggregation, quarantine and reauthorize the revoked packet, and publish only policy-permitted partial results.

questions.prompt:
A lead coordinates six jurisdiction specialists in parallel. Each worker has a separate OAuth scope; five return complete evidence packets, while one worker retrieves its packet and then loses its scope before synthesis. Organization policy requires access to remain valid at aggregation for every mandatory region.

Which aggregation policy handles the revoked worker without making an unsupported completeness claim?

constraints: The industry investigations are independent during research.
A lead must reconcile evidence and produce one final report.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Parallel workers consume more coordination and model budget, but they reduce elapsed research time when the tasks are genuinely independent.
details.errorCorrection: Separate independent exploration from final reconciliation instead of assuming concurrency alone creates a coherent report.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A multi-agent orchestrator assigns independent objectives, collects artifacts, and invokes a lead synthesis step after the worker barrier.
details.scenarioApplication: Each industry worker returns sources, assumptions, and findings in a common schema; the lead compares overlaps, resolves conflicts, and cites the selected evidence.
details.transfer: Use specialist workers for separable evidence gathering and reserve a lead or coordinator for ownership, synthesis, and unresolved conflicts.

messages.text: One large request hides per-industry failures and creates an unbounded context and synthesis problem.
Without scoped outputs and ownership, the lead cannot reliably reconcile or attribute the worker findings.
Sequential execution gives up the available independence and delays the report without improving the required synthesis contract.

feedback.reason: Independent research can run concurrently, but synthesis and conflict handling need one coordinating lead. Scoped workers and structured handoffs preserve both parallel throughput and report ownership.

options.text: Send all industry questions and source material in one large Claude request, then ask the model to separate the findings by industry.
Have independent workers run without a shared report contract and let the lead infer which findings belong in the final synthesis.
Run bounded specialist workers in parallel with scoped objectives and structured reports, then have a lead reconcile sources and produce the final report.
Use one sequential worker for every industry and merge its prose manually after all twelve investigations finish.

questions.prompt: A strategy team must investigate twelve industries concurrently, using a specialist per industry, and deliver one report reconciled by a lead. Which orchestration design matches the work?

constraints: Invoice cases are independent during extraction.
Every result needs deterministic validation before posting.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Per-item validation and quarantine reduce straight-through rate and require more records, but they prevent one malformed extraction from becoming a financial posting.
details.errorCorrection: Parallelize the independent unit, but put the side-effect gate after each unit rather than treating a batch result as inherently safe.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The orchestrator creates per-invoice jobs and correlation IDs; a deterministic gate consumes each result before the posting tool can mutate the ledger.
details.scenarioApplication: Limit concurrency to provider capacity, collect item outcomes, validate required fields and business rules, and route failed invoices for correction.
details.transfer: For independent repetitive work, use bounded fanout with isolated artifacts and preserve a deterministic per-item gate before side effects.

messages.text: A shared mutable ledger creates races and makes ownership or duplicate updates difficult to diagnose.
One context loses per-invoice isolation, increases context load, and does not improve the required validation boundary.
Posting before validation makes the audit report too late to prevent a bad external mutation.
Without bounded isolated fanout, independent invoices cannot use concurrency without losing correlation or overloading the service.
Without per-item deterministic validation, malformed or invalid model output can reach the posting side effect.

feedback.reason: Independent cases support bounded fanout, while the external posting boundary requires a validator for every item. Isolation and evidence-preserving quarantine keep failures attributable.

options.text: Share a mutable invoice ledger among workers and let whichever worker finishes last update the record.
Fan out bounded, isolated invoice tasks with a per-item correlation ID and aggregate their results after the workers finish.
Ask one agent to process all invoices in a single context so it can compare supplier patterns.
Allow a worker to post a result immediately when its extraction is fluent, then run validation as an audit report.
Run schema and business validation for each result before posting, and quarantine failures with their source and worker evidence.

questions.prompt: A finance team must process 100 independent invoices concurrently. Each extraction must pass a deterministic schema and business validator before any posting. Which TWO orchestration decisions fit? Select TWO.

constraints: The number and dependency structure emerge during inspection.
Each module needs scoped evidence, but the next task can change from findings.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Dynamic decomposition adds orchestration state and less predictable planning, but it avoids arbitrary batches that cause conflicts or miss hidden modules.
details.errorCorrection: Do not freeze decomposition before observing the dependency graph; make task creation responsive while keeping scopes and integration checks explicit.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Inspection produces a task graph; the coordinator assigns module scope, records prerequisites, and expands or sequences work based on returned findings.
details.scenarioApplication: Start with repository inventory, create a module task with its dependency evidence, validate each change, and enqueue newly revealed dependents only after their prerequisites pass.
details.transfer: Use adaptive task boundaries when discovery changes the work graph, with a coordinator that preserves ownership and prerequisite evidence.

messages.text: Equal batches ignore discovered dependencies and can make later edits run against an incompatible or incomplete migration state.
One context cannot provide scoped ownership or adapt its plan cleanly as module dependencies emerge.
File-count splits do not represent module dependencies and concurrent writes defer predictable conflicts to the merge.

feedback.reason: The right units and order are discovered rather than known up front. An orchestrator can decompose from evidence and maintain dependency-aware scheduling as the migration unfolds.

options.text: Predefine equal-sized module batches and execute them in a fixed order regardless of discovered dependencies.
Send the whole repository to one worker and ask it to keep every module change in one context.
Split by file count and run all changes concurrently, merging conflicts after the migration is complete.
Let an orchestrator inspect the repository, create scoped module tasks from discovered dependencies, and schedule the next task only when its prerequisites are satisfied.

questions.prompt: A repository migration has an unknown number of module-specific database and API changes; inspection reveals different dependencies and the next module to change depends on what the previous inspection finds. Which decomposition boundary fits?

constraints: The risk dimensions are separable checks.
The release recommendation is incomplete if any dimension is missing.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Focused checks produce more artifacts and coordination, but they reduce blind spots and allow a missed dimension to be diagnosed directly.
details.errorCorrection: Decompose by independent decision dimensions rather than prompt length, and verify coverage explicitly at the integration point.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Independent reviewers receive a precise risk contract and return evidence; an aggregator verifies that all required categories have results and flags conflicts.
details.scenarioApplication: Record findings by category and asset, require source evidence, and prevent the release recommendation from being marked complete until all three checks return.
details.transfer: When a composite review misses one aspect, split the mental model into named checks and add a completeness criterion to the final decision.

messages.text: A longer general prompt does not create ownership or evidence that the dependency dimension was actually checked.
Repeating only the missing check without a complete contract leaves coverage and interaction between all required dimensions unverified.
Sentence boundaries are not risk boundaries and arbitrary ownership can leave categories unreviewed or duplicated.

feedback.reason: The missed dependency dimension is a coverage failure. Explicit task ownership and a completeness gate make each required risk check visible before the recommendation.

options.text: Ask one longer prompt to discuss security generally and rely on its final confidence to show that all dimensions were considered.
Run only the dependency check because the other dimensions already appeared in earlier reviews.
Create focused checks for authentication, data exposure, and dependencies with explicit outputs, then use a completeness gate before the release recommendation.
Split the prompt by sentence position and let each worker invent which risk category it should inspect.

questions.prompt: A security review prompt covers authentication and data exposure but repeatedly misses dependency vulnerabilities. All three findings are required for one release recommendation. What decomposition should repair the gap?

constraints: The asset inventory is a prerequisite for all control checks.
The three control layers are independent after inventory validation and all evidence needs review.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The initial inventory gate delays fanout, but it prevents inconsistent asset scope and makes the final assessment reproducible.
details.errorCorrection: Order tasks by actual prerequisites, not control number or convenience, and preserve evidence at every decomposition boundary.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A validated prerequisite is distributed to independent tasks; each returns control-level evidence and an aggregator checks coverage and contradictions.
details.scenarioApplication: Freeze the inventory version, assign controls to access, encryption, or logging checks, retain evidence links, and review the complete set before certification.
details.transfer: For large assessments, model prerequisite artifacts and evidence gates explicitly before parallelizing independent checks.

messages.text: Workers using inconsistent inventories can produce incompatible scope and make later reconciliation unreliable.
Numeric order has no relationship to the shared inventory dependency or layer independence and only adds serial delay.
A single percentage hides missing controls and cannot support an evidence-based certification decision.

feedback.reason: The dependency requires a topological schedule: shared inventory first, independent layer work next, and an evidence barrier before the aggregate conclusion.

options.text: Launch all 400 checks immediately against whatever asset inventory each worker happens to load, then reconcile asset names later.
Run the controls sequentially in numeric order so later checks inherit the narrative from earlier ones.
Validate and version the shared inventory first, fan out isolated layer checks with evidence IDs, then run a cross-layer completeness and evidence review.
Ask one agent to inspect the entire control set and report one compliance percentage without preserving layer evidence.

questions.prompt: A controls assessment covers 400 controls. Every control depends on a shared asset inventory; after that inventory is validated, controls can be grouped into independent access, encryption, and logging checks before one evidence review. Which schedule is correct?

constraints: Most messages need only the coarse label.
Deep synthesis is required for a measured safety subset and must remain traceable to source messages.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Filtering may miss a safety case if the first-stage recall is weak, so the labeler needs a held-out recall check and a review path for uncertain labels.
details.errorCorrection: Allocate expensive reasoning to a validated subset and preserve the path from aggregate output back to the individual evidence.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A first-stage label partitions the corpus, a predicate selects the high-risk cluster, and a second-stage synthesis produces traceable evidence and escalation artifacts.
details.scenarioApplication: Store message IDs and label versions, pass only selected safety cases to deep analysis, and retain citations and decisions for reviewer audit.
details.transfer: For high-volume data, decompose into a cheap broad pass, evidence-based filter, and focused deep operation when the risk subset is identifiable.

messages.text: Deep synthesis for every message spends the expensive path on routine traffic and ignores the measured safety subset.
An unlinked sample cannot support an escalation decision or show whether the coarse filter found the risky cases.
Discarding labels and source links removes the traceability needed to validate the safety report.

feedback.reason: Map, filter, and reduce match the workload shape: inexpensive classification handles the majority, while the safety subset receives deeper analysis with lineage.

options.text: Map all messages to coarse labels, filter the safety clusters, run deep synthesis only on that subset, and retain links from every result to its source messages.
Run deep synthesis on all messages so the platform never risks missing a safety example.
Sample a few messages from each label and publish a safety rate without preserving which messages were escalated.
Let one agent summarize batches of messages and discard the coarse labels once it has produced a fluent report.

questions.prompt: A support platform has 2 million messages. A cheap first pass can assign coarse labels, but only messages in safety-related clusters need deep synthesis and an escalation packet. Which decomposition is proportionate?

constraints: Each record has all required fields and uses the same fixed checks and result contract.
No record depends on another record or a shared generated artifact.
Bounded fanout has been measured at 90 seconds versus 11 minutes serially.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If a generated schema or shared vocabulary became a prerequisite for every record, create that stage and run only the dependent checks afterward.
details.errorCorrection: There is no shared artifact for the records to consume, so the added stage only serializes work and introduces an unnecessary failure point.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic describes parallelization as running independent subtasks concurrently and aggregating their outputs programmatically. The scenario's mechanism is governed by this decisive constraint: With no prerequisite or cross-record dependency, independent checks should be decomposed for parallel execution rather than forced through a prerequisite stage.
details.scenarioApplication: Map records to independent validation tasks, run them with bounded concurrency, aggregate by record ID, and apply one completeness and error gate before release.
details.transfer: Use measured evidence and the stated authority boundary to choose the least complex design that satisfies the workload's constraint; revisit the route when the counterfactual changes.

messages.text: There is no shared artifact for the records to consume, so the added stage only serializes work and introduces an unnecessary failure point.
Serial execution ignores the measured independent work and the missing aggregation gate makes omissions or partial errors harder to detect.
Independent execution is appropriate, but publishing arrivals without checking completeness and errors can release a partial or invalid migration.

feedback.reason: The absence of dependencies makes parallel decomposition the simpler and faster choice while preserving a complete aggregate contract.

options.text: Fan out independent validation tasks with bounded concurrency, aggregate by record ID, and gate release on completeness and errors.
Create a shared terminology stage first, then fan out mappings that consume it as in a dependency-aware workflow.
Run all records serially to simplify ordering, then release the completed list without a separate aggregation gate.
Fan out every record and post each result as it arrives, without waiting for a final completeness and error gate.

questions.prompt:
A migration validates 10,000 independent records. Every record has all required schema fields, checks the same fixed rules, and returns the same result contract; no record depends on another record or a shared generated term list.

Which decomposition and release gate fit these independent records?

constraints: A precheck clears 1,080 controls; the remaining 120 failures form eight observed causes.
All four diagnostic schemas together add 14,000 tokens to the 10,000-token case, while the selected schema adds 3,000.
Each cause needs one owner and further decomposition only when evidence is contradictory.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the case evidence fell to 2,000 tokens or all four schemas became mandatory for one cause, recalculate admission; if the request still exceeds 16,000, queue or narrow it instead of evicting mandatory evidence.
details.errorCorrection: The eager surface adds 14,000 tokens to a 10,000-token case, exceeds the 16,000-token input budget before output reserve, and duplicates work for 1,080 controls already cleared.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends loading the most critical tools while deferring others for discovery when the tool inventory is large. The scenario's mechanism is governed by this decisive constraint: Decomposition must follow observed failure clusters and admit only the tool schema needed for the assigned cause so the 16,000-token budget and output reserve remain intact.
details.scenarioApplication: Run the precheck, assign one bounded owner per failing cause, use governed deferred tool discovery to expose only the selected 3,000-token schema for that cause, and spawn a further focused task only for a concrete contradiction before aggregating the eight packets.
details.transfer: Use measured evidence and the stated authority boundary to choose the least complex design that satisfies the workload's constraint; revisit the route when the counterfactual changes.

messages.text: The eager surface adds 14,000 tokens to a 10,000-token case, exceeds the 16,000-token input budget before output reserve, and repeats work for controls already cleared.
Centralizing all schemas still consumes the same over-budget tool surface and delays evidence-based selection; it violates the bounded request and ownership design.
This ignores the observed eight-cause clusters, loses bounded cause ownership, and repeats context and tool admission beyond the 16,000-token budget.

feedback.reason: The numeric budget makes capability admission part of the decomposition boundary: the work is grouped by evidence and the tool surface is selected per group.

options.text: Create one agent and expose all four diagnostic schemas for every control so any failure can call any tool immediately.
Precheck and group failures by cause, assign bounded owners, discover only each selected schema, and split further only for contradictions.
Give one coordinator all four schemas and let it decide which cause to investigate after inspecting the entire case.
Run each of the 120 failing controls independently with full diagnostic context and merge the results manually.

questions.prompt:
A compliance audit has 1,200 controls. A deterministic precheck clears 1,080, while 120 failures cluster into eight causes. The request input budget is 16,000 tokens: current case evidence uses 10,000, and all four rare diagnostic tool schemas add 14,000, while the selected schema for one cause adds 3,000.

Which decomposition and tool-admission plan fits the clustered failures and 16,000-token budget?

constraints: The terminology table is a shared prerequisite.
Endpoint mappings are independent after it and all must pass one compatibility gate.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: More task records and a final barrier add orchestration work, but they allow concurrency without losing consistent terminology or cross-endpoint validation.
details.errorCorrection: Split by meaningful business units and preserve shared prerequisites; arbitrary chunking or premature aggregation hides dependency errors.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A shared prerequisite artifact feeds isolated subtasks; an aggregate compatibility gate consumes all outputs and can identify the endpoint that failed.
details.scenarioApplication: Version the terminology table, assign one endpoint and correlation ID per worker, and run schema or compatibility checks before release.
details.transfer: For complex work, identify shared inputs, independent units, and integration gates before choosing task boundaries.

messages.text: One narrative obscures endpoint-level errors and makes the shared vocabulary and compatibility checks difficult to verify.
Token ranges do not correspond to endpoint ownership and can split terms or schemas without preserving the shared contract.
A compatibility gate that runs before all mappings arrive cannot validate the complete interface.

feedback.reason: The decomposition follows the dependency graph: establish common vocabulary, process independent endpoints, and validate the combined contract.

options.text: Give one agent the entire endpoint set and ask it to preserve terminology and compatibility in one final narrative.
Resolve the shared terminology contract first, decompose into isolated endpoint mapping tasks, then run the compatibility check over the collected results.
Split each endpoint into arbitrary token ranges and merge the partial mappings without a shared vocabulary artifact.
Run endpoint mapping and compatibility validation concurrently so the gate can finish before all mappings arrive.

questions.prompt: An API migration must map 80 endpoints. All mappings use one terminology table, then can be checked independently before a compatibility gate. Which decomposition is most useful?

constraints: Retention, access, and minimization have distinct evidence and checks.
The release owner needs complete, attributable results before deciding.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The gate can delay a release when one check is late or conflicting, but it prevents the owner from deciding on partial privacy evidence.
details.errorCorrection: Separate independent checks while making the integration requirement explicit; do not replace coverage with one broad narrative or unrelated approvals.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A decomposition contract assigns each reviewer an explicit dimension and shared identifiers; an aggregator checks presence, provenance, and contradictions before handoff.
details.scenarioApplication: Review the same data inventory under retention, access, and minimization rules, link findings to assets, and block release readiness until all reports pass the gate.
details.transfer: For composite governance decisions, decompose by criterion and require an evidence-complete aggregation before the accountable owner acts.

messages.text: A broad narrative hides omissions and gives the owner no reliable way to tell whether each privacy dimension was checked.
A classification label cannot establish current retention, access, and minimization behavior for every asset.
Independent readiness decisions create competing authority and do not ensure that all required findings reached the owner.
Without scoped dimension checks, evidence ownership and coverage cannot be audited or compared across the review.
Without a completeness and conflict gate, the release owner may act on a missing or contradictory privacy finding.

feedback.reason: The dimensions are distinct units, while the owner needs a complete combined decision. Scoped evidence and a final gate provide both independence and completeness.

options.text: Ask one reviewer to produce a broad privacy narrative and let the owner infer which checks it covered.
Assign one scoped check to each privacy dimension with a shared asset and policy context, then preserve a correlation ID for each result.
Run minimization only because retention and access can be assumed from the data classification label.
Let each reviewer decide release readiness independently so the owner can choose the most favorable conclusion.
Use a completeness and conflict gate that verifies all three findings before the release owner receives a decision packet.

questions.prompt: A privacy review must check retention, access, and data minimization independently, but every finding is required before one release owner decides. Which TWO decomposition choices are appropriate? Select TWO.

constraints: The opportunity depends on discovering new paths in a changing corpus.
Citations, budget limits, and human review are required before action.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The evaluated pilot costs more and may leave findings pending review, but it tests the transformational hypothesis without making exploration an uncontrolled action path.
details.errorCorrection: Match transformation claims to a measurable capability and preserve a review boundary for uncertain or consequential findings.
details.mechanismOrProperty: An agent can choose follow-up searches as findings change; budgets, source records, evaluation cases, and a human gate constrain the exploratory path.
details.scenarioApplication: Measure discovery recall, citation support, time, spend, and reviewer acceptance on representative research tasks before expanding the pilot.
details.transfer: For high-upside discovery, define the evidence, budget, and human decision boundary as part of the value case rather than as post-launch cleanup.

messages.text: A fixed path may be efficient but cannot adapt to the discovery-dependent work described and would publish without the required review.
Unrestricted exploration lacks a spending and evidence boundary and crosses the human action requirement.
Document count is an activity measure; it does not establish a useful discovery or supported conclusion.

feedback.reason: Open-ended discovery is where adaptive exploration can create transformational value, but the pilot needs evidence, stop conditions, and human ownership before action.

options.text: Use a fixed retrieval workflow and publish its first answer as the discovery result so cost and latency remain predictable.
Open the full corpus to an unrestricted agent and let it act on a novel finding without an evidence or spending boundary.
Pilot an evaluated agentic research path with bounded searches, source citations, cost tracking, and human review of the proposed conclusion.
Optimize only the number of documents searched and treat broad corpus coverage as transformation regardless of finding quality.

questions.prompt: A research group seeks potentially transformational discovery across a changing corpus. Exploration is open-ended and a human must review evidence before any conclusion is acted on. Which value-aligned design should be piloted?

constraints: Completion is high but does not reflect reviewer effort or outcome quality.
The current process can provide a baseline for resolution and handling time.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Richer measurement requires labeling and instrumentation, but it distinguishes a valuable draft from a fluent draft that adds work.
details.errorCorrection: Measure the business process end to end, including human correction, rather than optimizing a model-output or completion counter.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Resolution and acceptance capture usefulness, while handling time and rework capture productivity; segmentation shows where the assistant helps or burdens agents.
details.scenarioApplication: Compare accepted answers, resolution and repeat contacts, minutes per case, and edits with a matched baseline before changing prompts or models.
details.transfer: Whenever a product metric stays high while users still work around the system, add outcome and effort measures tied to the current process.

messages.text: Raising a proxy threshold does not address the unchanged handling time or reveal whether conversations actually resolve.
Generated volume can increase editing burden and says nothing about acceptance or customer outcome.
Rewriting identifies a possible defect but not whether a targeted prompt, route, or workflow change could recover value.

feedback.reason: Completion is a weak proxy when human rewriting consumes the supposed time benefit. The next diagnosis must measure the actual work and outcome against current practice.

options.text: Increase the completion target to 98% and treat the higher percentage as proof that the assistant creates productivity.
Measure resolution, accepted-answer rate, handling time, and rework against the current process, segmented by conversation type.
Count generated words and use longer answers as evidence that the assistant addresses more customer needs.
Replace the model immediately because any rewriting means the AI path has no business value.

questions.prompt: A dashboard reports that 92% of conversations completed, but agents spend the same time because they rewrite many answers before sending them. Which measurement diagnosis should guide the next change?

constraints: The measured speed gain is paired with a material resolution regression.
The target resolution floor is 82% and slices can be evaluated before broad rollout.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Expansion pauses and analysis costs time, but it avoids scaling a fast workflow that drives repeat contacts and damages service value.
details.errorCorrection: Treat speed and outcome quality as a joint business constraint and use failure slices to target the smallest corrective change.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Segmented evaluation can locate failure classes such as policy gaps or unsafe confidence; routing, prompt, retrieval, or review changes can then be tested against both SLA pillars.
details.scenarioApplication: Hold broad rollout, compare resolution and handle time by intent and customer segment, and accept a revised path only when it clears the 82% floor without unacceptable effort.
details.transfer: When efficiency improves while outcome quality falls, keep both measures in the gate and diagnose the work slice before choosing rollout or redesign.

messages.text: Handle time alone ignores the resolution target and accepts a workflow that shifts effort into repeat contacts.
A full permanent rollback discards potentially recoverable value before identifying whether one slice or route causes the regression.
Changing the target hides a measured failure instead of bringing the service back to the agreed business floor.

feedback.reason: A faster interaction that fails to resolve the contact misses the service value target. The next step is a slice diagnosis and measured revision, not a single-metric rollout or an unscoped permanent rollback.

options.text: Keep the release because handle-time improvement is the clearest efficiency signal, and address repeat contacts after adoption grows.
Roll back every AI feature permanently because one aggregate outcome regressed without testing where the regression occurs.
Pause broad expansion, segment the resolution failures, and retest a scoped prompt, retrieval, or human route until the 82% floor and acceptable handling time are jointly met.
Raise the resolution target in the dashboard to match the observed result while continuing the same design.

questions.prompt: A contact-center assistant reduces average handle time by 18%, but first-contact resolution falls from 84% to 72% and repeat contacts increase. The target is at least 82% first-contact resolution. What decision should follow?

constraints: The current evidence covers acceptance but not operational or downstream value.
Broader deployment can wait for a defined measurement gate.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A longer pilot delays scale and requires outcome follow-up, but it protects the insurer from optimizing summaries that save no time or alter claim quality adversely.
details.errorCorrection: Do not turn early approval into a broad productivity claim; define the operational and downstream measures before increasing exposure.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A pilot can connect summary versions to adjuster behavior, decision time, corrections, and later claim outcomes, producing a balanced value evaluation.
details.scenarioApplication: Instrument representative adjusters and claim slices, compare with current practice, and expand only if quality remains acceptable while time and downstream outcomes improve.
details.transfer: For AI features with indirect business effects, measure adoption, effort, corrections, and downstream outcomes before calling a pilot successful.

messages.text: Acceptance does not establish adoption, time-to-decision, correction burden, or downstream claim quality at scale.
Token cost is one constraint and cannot replace the quality and operational measures needed for the business decision.
Generation volume measures activity, not whether adjusters use the summaries or whether claims resolve better.

feedback.reason: Acceptance is useful but incomplete. The business case concerns adoption, time, correction burden, and claim outcomes, so expansion needs a measurement gate for those effects.

options.text: Extend the pilot with measures for adjuster adoption, time-to-decision, correction rate, and downstream outcomes, then gate expansion on predefined thresholds.
Expand to every adjuster because acceptance of the summaries proves that the insurer will realize productivity value.
Stop measuring and select the model with the lowest token cost so the pilot cannot exceed budget.
Use the number of summaries generated as the expansion criterion and infer claim quality from coverage.

questions.prompt: An insurer pilots Claude summaries for adjusters. Managers want broader deployment, but the pilot has only summary acceptance data; adoption, time-to-decision, correction rate, and downstream claim outcomes were not measured. What value decision is appropriate?

constraints: The efficient model scores 91% and the stronger model 98% on the same held-out exception set.
At least 97% recall of material exceptions is required.
High-impact appeals are a minority and a human path remains available; the stronger route meets the asynchronous deadline.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the efficient model cleared 97% on the same held-out slice, use it as the default and test a stronger route only for measured residual failures.
details.errorCorrection: The efficient path misses the material-exception floor and shifts error cost into appeals without meeting the business outcome.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends evaluating model capabilities, speed, cost, and effort against the actual use case rather than optimizing one dimension alone. The scenario's mechanism is governed by this decisive constraint: The material-exception quality floor is a hard business requirement, so efficiency cannot justify a path that fails it.
details.scenarioApplication: Use the stronger model for the exception workload or route it to a validated stronger or human path, and retain the efficient model only where its measured quality clears the applicable floor.
details.transfer: Use measured evidence and the stated authority boundary to choose the least complex design that satisfies the workload's constraint; revisit the route when the counterfactual changes.

messages.text: The efficient path misses the material-exception floor and shifts error cost into appeals without meeting the business outcome.
The stronger model clears the exception floor, but applying its four-times unit cost to every case ignores the stated minority workload and available allocation boundary.
Random sampling does not ensure the material-exception slice clears 97%; the measured failure is already known and should drive the route.

feedback.reason: Value alignment can favor higher capability when a consequence-bearing quality floor is explicit and the route remains operationally feasible.

options.text: Use the efficient model for all appeals because its lower cost maximizes productivity.
Use the stronger model for every appeal because quality is hard, and defer any cost or workload segmentation review.
Use the stronger route for exception cases, keeping the efficient model only where its measured quality clears the floor.
Route a random quarter of appeals to the stronger model and accept efficient output for the rest until an incident identifies a quality problem.

questions.prompt:
A tax-appeal assistant must recall at least 97% of material exceptions. The efficient model reaches 91%, while a stronger model reaches 98% at four times the unit cost and remains under the asynchronous service deadline.

Which model allocation satisfies the material-exception quality requirement?

constraints: Both models were measured on the same routine and high-impact classes.
