Classifier uncertainty has a reviewer path; the measured segmented route costs $2,300 and the stronger model is used for 10,000 high-impact cases.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the stronger route measured above 2.5 seconds end to end under the routed load, reject that route for the hard-deadline slice and use a reviewed asynchronous or narrower escalation path; if its cost fell below the global budget, broaden only after the same class gates pass.
details.errorCorrection: All-stronger exceeds the $2,500 budget by $5,000, while all-efficient misses the 95% high-impact floor; the stronger route is feasible at 2.3 seconds only for the high-impact slice.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends evaluating model capabilities, speed, cost, and effort against the actual use case rather than optimizing one dimension alone. The scenario's mechanism is governed by this decisive constraint: Both models were measured on the same classes, so the decision must satisfy the 95% high-impact floor, 2.5-second p95 limit, and $2,500 monthly budget together.
details.scenarioApplication: Use the efficient model for routine cases and the stronger model for identified high-impact cases, confirm the routed mix stays under the 2.5-second end-to-end p95 and $2,500 budget, and send classifier-uncertain high-impact cases to the bounded reviewer queue.
details.transfer: Use measured evidence and the stated authority boundary to choose the least complex design that satisfies the workload's constraint; revisit the route when the counterfactual changes.

messages.text: The efficient model scores only 91% on high-impact cases, below the 95% hard floor, so its lower cost cannot justify an all-efficient route.
The all-stronger route costs $7,500 per month and exceeds the $2,500 budget even though its latency and quality are acceptable.
Classifier precision and predicted classes do not replace end-to-end slice quality; unresolved high-impact uncertainty needs the bounded reviewer path.

feedback.reason: The worked monthly costs and same-class outcomes make segmented routing the only stated design that meets the high-impact floor without exceeding budget or latency.

options.text: Use the efficient model for all 50,000 cases because its $1,000 monthly cost is lowest.
Use the stronger model for every case because its 96% high-impact score clears the quality floor.
Route every case solely from the classifier, send no uncertainty cases to review, and accept the predicted class as the quality measure.
Route routine cases to the efficient model and high-impact cases to the stronger model, with budget, p95, quality, and reviewer gates.

questions.prompt:
A claims triage service handles 50,000 cases per month: 40,000 routine and 10,000 high-impact cases. On the same held-out routine and high-impact classes, the efficient model scores 97% and 91%, costs $0.02 per case, and runs at 1.2 seconds p95; the stronger model scores 98% and 96%, costs $0.15, and runs at 2.3 seconds p95.

Which model route satisfies the shared quality, latency, budget, and uncertainty constraints?

constraints: The service has a latency and unit-cost target.
Both candidates need task-quality evidence and staff escalation remains available.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The default path may automate fewer difficult cases, but it protects SLA and budget while generating evidence for a targeted upgrade.
details.errorCorrection: Align the architecture to the business value pillars and measured constraints instead of treating autonomy or price as a proxy for value.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A workload-specific benchmark links model pattern to latency, spend, quality, and escalation; the route makes a human or stronger path available where the efficient path is insufficient.
details.scenarioApplication: Measure answer correctness, p95, cost per question, and escalation on routine and difficult slices before setting the efficient path as the default.
details.transfer: When choosing among AI designs, compare task quality, speed, spend, and operational workload on the slice that creates the proposed value.

messages.text: Transformation language does not override a measured SLA and cost failure, and it provides no evidence that the extra autonomy helps the product-question task.
Price alone cannot establish useful answer quality or a safe default for customers.
Duplicate execution adds cost and answer length is not a business outcome or correctness measure.

feedback.reason: The efficient design meets the stated performance and cost constraints, but quality still needs evidence. Routing difficult cases preserves service value without paying the agentic cost for routine traffic.

options.text: Choose the agentic design because more autonomous steps signal greater transformation even though its measured latency and cost miss the target.
Choose the efficient design solely from price and skip quality measurement because retrieval is already familiar.
Run both designs for every customer and let answer length determine which one creates more value.
Use the efficient candidate for routine questions, verify its quality on representative cases, and route measured uncertainty or difficult cases to staff or a stronger path.

questions.prompt: A retailer compares two designs for product questions. An efficient retrieval workflow measures 1.8 seconds p95 and meets the unit-cost budget; an agentic workflow measures 6.4 seconds p95 and exceeds it. Which initial decision aligns the solution with value?

constraints: Review and cleanup are part of the engineering work.
The goal is a faster, higher-quality end-to-end change process.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The measures require review labels and longer observation windows, but they prevent a high-volume generator from appearing productive while increasing cycle time.
details.errorCorrection: Replace activity counts with measures that include human correction and the business process outcome the assistant is meant to improve.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Outcome measures join model output to reviewer disposition and repository completion; a baseline comparison reveals whether assistance reduces total engineering effort.
details.scenarioApplication: Track accepted-change rate by task type and elapsed request-to-merge time including review and rework against a matched non-assistant baseline.
details.transfer: For AI-assisted work, measure what users accept and how long the complete job takes, not how much text the model emits.

messages.text: Suggestion volume rewards generation even when reviewers reject or rewrite the output and does not measure completed work.
Response length is not code quality or engineering productivity and can increase review burden.
Touched-file count can reflect noisy or harmful changes and has no relationship to accepted delivery time.
Without accepted-change rate, the team cannot tell whether generated suggestions are useful enough to keep.
Without end-to-end cycle time including review and rework, the dashboard can miss a productivity loss caused by cleanup.

feedback.reason: Accepted changes capture usefulness and cycle time captures the full productivity effect, including review and cleanup. Suggestion volume can rise while the process gets slower.

options.text: Accepted-change rate on representative suggestions, including the proportion merged with no substantive rewrite.
Total suggestions generated per developer, regardless of whether a change is accepted or useful.
Average response length, because longer code explanations indicate more capable assistance.
Number of files touched by each suggestion, even when reviewers revert the change.
End-to-end cycle time from request through review and rework to an accepted change, compared with the current workflow.

questions.prompt: A coding assistant produces many suggestions, but reviewers reject a large share and cleanup extends the engineering cycle. Which TWO measures should replace suggestion volume as the primary value signal? Select TWO.

constraints: Representative investigations can be evaluated by the research team.
Cost optimization will follow only after the task-quality floor is established.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: For a high-volume routine task with tight operating budgets, an efficient candidate may be the appropriate first benchmark; this pilot has different priorities.
details.errorCorrection: A weak starting model can create a false negative about feasibility, while general benchmarks and component-level accuracy do not establish the quality of the complete investigation.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends a capability-first starting point for complex reasoning and accuracy-sensitive work, followed by evaluation and efficiency optimization.
details.scenarioApplication: Evaluate representative investigations with the strongest suitable configuration, inspect the quality boundary, and compare lower-cost configurations only against that established standard.
details.transfer: Choose the initial evaluation baseline according to the uncertainty being resolved: capability feasibility or operating efficiency.

messages.text: Failure of the cheapest model does not establish that the task is infeasible with suitable capability.
Fixing the tier from unrelated benchmarks precedes the task-specific evidence that the team needs.

questions.prompt:

Which admission policy protects the useful request under the 32,000-token limit?

constraints: Full contract text and document metadata are available.
The next question’s relevant clauses are not known in advance.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: As the corpus grows beyond useful context, select or retrieve relevant evidence rather than retaining every document indiscriminately.
details.errorCorrection: Flattened text and positional identifiers weaken provenance, while fixed abstracts can omit the clause needed for an unpredictable later question.
details.mechanismOrProperty: For long context, Anthropic recommends putting long-form data near the top, structuring documents with descriptive tags, and placing the query near the end.
details.scenarioApplication: Use explicit document and section identifiers with the full relevant text, then state the comparison question and citation requirements after the documents.
details.transfer: Preserve source identity and useful evidence when organizing long context; reduce irrelevant material rather than merely maximizing input volume.

messages.text: The continuous block weakens explicit source boundaries, and it does not follow the documented documents-before-query organization for long material.
An equal-length abstract can remove the decisive clause before the question is known; answer-style examples do not restore that evidence.
Position is fragile provenance, and repeated questions add tokens without providing stable document or section identity.

feedback.reason: Structured document context keeps source material addressable, and the final changing query gives the model a clear task after that material. Destructive abstraction is unnecessary while the required evidence fits.

options.text: Place the changing question first and append the contracts as one continuous text block, relying on their legal titles to distinguish sources.
Put labeled documents and metadata before the changing question and response instructions, preserving source identity and removing irrelevant material as needed.
Replace every contract with an equally sized abstract and use the saved tokens for several examples of the desired answer style.
Order contracts by length and repeat the question between them, using positional order as the citation identifier.

questions.prompt: An analyst compares six long contracts that fit the available context budget. Relevant clauses may occur anywhere, and each answer must distinguish the documents and cite its evidence. The analyst’s question changes on each request. How should the request be organized?

constraints: The active objective, confirmed findings, decisions, and unresolved dependencies must survive.
Stored sensor identifiers can retrieve detailed readings later.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Unique evidence that cannot be retrieved again must be preserved deliberately; the reference strategy relies on the stated durable sensor store.
details.errorCorrection: Conversation length is not a durable state contract, a recommendation omits its dependencies, and an irreversible narrative reduction can remove evidence needed by a later hypothesis.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic describes just-in-time context retrieval: retain lightweight identifiers and dynamically load detailed information only when relevant.
details.scenarioApplication: Write notes with the objective, confirmed facts, decisions, unresolved dependencies, and next actions. Retain identifiers for sensor evidence that can be loaded on demand.
details.transfer: Separate the state required for continuity from the detailed evidence that can be retrieved when needed.

messages.text: A growing transcript competes with the active task and still needs a reliable state transfer when the session refreshes.
A machine name and latest recommendation do not encode the unresolved dependencies or rationale needed to continue correctly.
A fixed narrative conclusion can lose measurements or uncertainty that become relevant to a different hypothesis.
Structured durable notes preserve the high-signal state needed after context refresh.
Lightweight references keep detailed evidence accessible without retaining every raw payload in the active window.

feedback.reason: Durable state preserves the investigation’s governing decisions, while retrievable references make detailed evidence available without repeatedly filling active context.

options.text: Persist structured high-signal notes describing the active state and next checks outside the conversation.
Keep an uninterrupted conversational transcript as the primary state record and increase the refresh interval to reduce reconstruction work.
Store only the latest recommendation and rely on the next model session to reconstruct its supporting dependencies from the machine name.
Keep lightweight sensor and artifact references, loading detailed readings when the current hypothesis requires them.
Replace all measurements with a compact narrative conclusion so every refresh receives the same minimal text.

questions.prompt: A field-service agent investigates a machine fault across many turns and session refreshes. Technicians need the current investigation to continue correctly, while large raw sensor payloads can be fetched again. Select TWO context strategies that support continuity.

constraints: Most requests do not need this procedure.
The procedure includes both guidance and executable resources.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If only a remote action interface were needed, a tool could be sufficient; this case requires reusable procedural instructions and resources.
details.errorCorrection: Always-loaded prompts and full tool descriptions impose unnecessary context costs; universal retrieval does not directly provide the requested packaged workflow.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Skills expose metadata first, load instructions when triggered, and load resources as needed.
details.scenarioApplication: Describe when the Skill applies in metadata, put the workflow in SKILL.md, and include the relevant scripts and reference files for access when needed.
details.transfer: Choose a reusable unit whose loading behavior fits when its instructions and resources are needed.

messages.text: The complete procedure loads even on unrelated requests, violating the small startup footprint.
Mandatory search on every conversation adds an unnecessary step and does not itself define the requested instruction-and-script package.
The complete description and repeated references defeat the requirement to load detailed material only when relevant.

feedback.reason: Skills support progressive disclosure of metadata, instructions, and resources, matching the requested reusable package and context-loading behavior.

options.text: Embed the complete procedure and reference text in the shared system prompt, and expose validation through a separate tool.
Package an Agent Skill with discoverable metadata, SKILL.md instructions, and supporting resources loaded as needed.
Store every procedure in a retrieval index and make semantic search the required first step of each conversation.
Provide a tool whose description contains all procedure instructions, with the reference files included in every tool result.

questions.prompt: Several teams need a reusable procedure with instructions, reference files, and validation scripts. Startup should expose only a short description; detailed instructions and resources should load when relevant. Which packaging best matches that requirement?

constraints: The executor already enforces the new schema.
Live user queries follow the cached prefix.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Frequently changing schemas reduce reuse; stabilize genuine interface contracts without concealing required changes.
details.errorCorrection: Restoring an obsolete schema or delaying a valid release treats cache reuse as more authoritative than the tool contract.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Prompt caching reuses matching prefix content; a changed tool or prompt block before the breakpoint creates a distinct prefix.
details.scenarioApplication: Send the new tool schema with the stable instructions, retain the query after the breakpoint, and compare cache behavior for requests with the same new prefix.
details.transfer: Distinguish expected cache invalidation from a tool-contract defect.

messages.text: The model would still see an obsolete interface and could omit a parameter the executor requires; preserving prefix bytes does not repair that mismatch.
The changing query would become part of the preceding content and reduce reuse rather than explaining the observed successful warm requests.
The new schema necessarily creates different prefix content regardless of when the former cache entry expires.

feedback.reason: The schema change changes prefix content. An initial miss followed by matching-prefix hits is consistent with normal cache behavior, while model and executor contracts must remain aligned.

options.text: Restore the old model-facing tool schema and translate omitted parameters in the executor to preserve the previous prefix.
Move the tool definitions behind each user query and investigate whether shorter role instructions restore the former hit rate.
Keep the updated model and executor schemas aligned, accept the changed prefix’s initial miss, and observe reuse on matching requests.
Roll back the schema release until the former cached prefix expires, then retry deployment with the same parameter requirement.

questions.prompt: An application caches role instructions and tool schemas. A release adds a required tool parameter, after which the first request misses the cache and subsequent identical-prefix requests hit. What response fits this evidence?

constraints: Answers must use the requesting tenant’s current entitlement policy.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Different tenant policy content may reduce shared-prefix reuse; preserve policy correctness rather than substituting another tenant’s content.
details.errorCorrection: Product-tier similarity, model inference, and session pinning do not satisfy the requirement for current tenant-specific entitlement rules.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Prompt caching reuses matching cumulative prefixes; placing tenant policy before the breakpoint makes version changes visible, while tenant scoping and privacy are requirements supplied by this scenario.
details.scenarioApplication: Resolve the policy using validated tenant identity and current version, assemble its actual content with the common instructions, and put the question after the breakpoint.
details.transfer: Treat tenant scoping and freshness as application responsibilities, and cache only the correctly assembled request content.

messages.text: A policy for the same product tier may have different private entitlements; an appended identity does not correct the selected policy.
A common summary can omit tenant-specific rules, and the customer question is not an authoritative source of those rules.
Session pinning can retain a superseded entitlement policy even after the tenant’s current version changes.

feedback.reason: The application must select the correct tenant and policy version before caching can optimize matching prefix content. Reuse does not establish authorization or policy freshness.

options.text: Select a recently cached entitlement policy with the same product tier, then append the validated tenant identity as a correction.
Use one shared entitlement summary for the cacheable portion and let the model resolve tenant-specific exceptions from the question.
Pin each tenant to its first policy prefix for the session and refresh only after the user explicitly asks about a policy change.
Assemble the current policy for the validated tenant after the common safety content, with the changing question after the cache breakpoint.

questions.prompt: A service shares identical safety instructions across tenants, but each tenant has private, independently versioned entitlement rules. The application has validated the tenant identity before assembling the prompt. How should it combine correct policy selection with prefix reuse?

constraints: The current catalog must be used immediately after publication.
The request supports cache breakpoints at appropriate content boundaries.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Breakpoints are useful only where matching prefixes recur; measure reuse rather than adding boundaries to content that rarely repeats.
details.errorCorrection: A changing question or catalog before stable material changes the cumulative prefix; session pinning also violates catalog freshness.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends placing static tools, system instructions, context, and examples before dynamic content and adding a breakpoint after the stable prefix.
details.scenarioApplication: Place the stable role and schema first, then weekly examples, then the current catalog with suitable breakpoints, and append the changing question after those reusable portions.
details.transfer: Arrange prompt content by stability while maintaining current authoritative data.

messages.text: The changing question invalidates the cumulative prefix from its beginning, preventing reuse of the intended stable content.
Waiting for a weekly refresh serves an outdated hourly catalog and violates immediate publication requirements.
An hourly catalog change before the stable instructions changes the cumulative prefix that includes those instructions.

feedback.reason: Ordering stable content before more volatile content preserves reusable earlier prefixes while current catalog bytes and the final question change independently.

options.text: Place the latest question first, followed by the catalog, examples, and role contract, with a breakpoint after the entire request.
Order content from stable contract through examples to current catalog, set breakpoints for reusable prefixes, and put the question last.

Put the hourly catalog before the stable instructions and cache only the complete prefix so every content layer has one refresh policy.

questions.prompt: A shopping assistant uses stable role instructions and an output schema, weekly examples, an hourly catalog, and a different question each time. Each layer receives enough repeated requests to benefit from reuse. What arrangement best preserves useful prefixes as content changes?

Which cache decision is correct for this prompt shape?

questions.prompt: A support assistant uses stable safety instructions, a tenant policy that becomes effective immediately when published, and a different customer question on every request. How should the application arrange the cached prefix?

constraints: Common instructions are identical across teams.
Specialized procedures are selected only when relevant.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A procedure used on virtually every request might justify more upfront context; the stated procedures are selectively needed.
details.errorCorrection: Universal inclusion wastes context, independent copies drift, and script names do not replace required procedural guidance.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Skills load needed files and bundle instructions, resources, and scripts without imposing their context cost before access.
details.scenarioApplication: Assemble the common role and output instructions consistently, then route relevant tasks to Skills that provide the specific workflow and resources.
details.transfer: Separate genuinely shared instructions from task-specific procedures according to their reuse and loading needs.

messages.text: Unrelated team procedures consume context on every request, contrary to selective loading.
Independent copies weaken the single shared contract and make consistency harder to maintain.

questions.prompt: A platform serves several teams with the same role and output contract. Each team also has a specialized procedure with instructions and scripts, needed only for routed tasks. Which choices preserve reuse while limiting unnecessary context? Select TWO.

constraints: The active context needs bounded relevant results.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The design may require another tool call for a broad question, but it protects attention and makes completeness an observable choice.

details.mechanismOrProperty: Programmatic filtering and pagination process results before model exposure; a continuation token and record-ID lookup provide deliberate expansion when the user needs it.

messages.text: Pagination alone still returns broad pages and leaves selection to the model; without claim-specific filters and a record-level detail contract, the relevant clause can remain buried and page requests become model-driven.

feedback.reason: The tool should constrain intermediate context without hiding valid evidence. Pagination and detail lookup preserve access to the full set while making the common claim query focused.

options.text: Return the complete result set in pages but place the first page in context and ask Claude to summarize before requesting more pages.

constraints: Each exposed capability should have one distinct operation and a predictable filter contract.

details.errorCorrection: Diagnose overlapping capability surfaces before adding prompt prose, retries, or unrestricted database access.

Arbitrary database access bypasses typed and authorized capability boundaries and makes the selection problem less observable.

feedback.reason: The defect is capability ambiguity: overlapping names and incompatible filters make a valid request map to the wrong contract. Canonical tools reduce choices and make parameters testable.

options.text: Add aliases and examples for all four tools so Claude has more wording clues while preserving the overlapping contracts.
Call all four tools for each request, compare their results, and let Claude choose the most complete invoice record.
Consolidate the overlapping surface into canonical identifier and search tools with distinct names, filters, and contract tests.

questions.prompt: A finance assistant has four tools named fetch_invoice, search_invoice, lookup_invoice, and retrieve_invoice. They accept different filters, overlap in purpose, and the assistant often selects a contract that cannot satisfy the request. What should be diagnosed first?

constraints: The visible workflow needs two narrow operations.

details.mechanismOrProperty: Typed narrow tools reduce the model-visible action space and allow application validation to reject unsupported combinations before an expensive or failing call.
details.scenarioApplication: Use an ID lookup for exact records and a date-bounded search for ranges, with required identifiers or dates and clear result contracts.
details.transfer: When a tool union creates invalid combinations, split by operation and validate the narrow contract before execution.

messages.text: Examples can guide selection but do not make incompatible optional fields impossible and leave retries as the error control.
Hiding modes while preserving the union still exposes the same parameter ambiguity and makes the schema disagree with the intended capability.
Normalizing after a service error spends a call and treats a preventable contract defect as runtime recovery.

feedback.reason: A union-shaped tool makes the model choose among combinations the workflow does not need. Two purpose-specific schemas make required fields and invalid modes explicit before execution.

options.text: Keep one universal tool with examples for common combinations, validate only after a service error, and let the model retry with a revised optional-field set.
Hide the four output modes in prose while retaining their union schema, then accept the model's selected mode when the backend can coerce it.
Split the surface into typed identifier-lookup and date-bounded-search tools with required fields, and remove unused modes from this workflow.

questions.prompt: A reporting tool exposes eighteen optional filters, four mutually exclusive output modes, and nullable identifiers. Malformed combinations cause retries, although this workflow needs only ID lookup and date-bounded search. Which redesign is best?

constraints: The aggregate must be complete and arithmetically correct.

messages.text: Raw rows pollute context and make completeness and arithmetic depend on the model receiving every event.
A random sample cannot answer a complete count and offers no path to verify a disputed event.
Free-form context-limited queries make result membership implicit and can expose more data than the audit question requires.

feedback.reason: The service can compute a complete aggregate without spending model context on every row, while IDs preserve an evidence path for drill-down.

options.text: Aggregate and filter in the service or programmatic tool, expose the summary and representative event IDs, and provide a separate bounded detail call.
Return the 100,000 events to a programmatic model tool, ask Claude to group them, and let the model choose drill-down IDs from its truncated context.
Use a statistically selected event sample to estimate actor/day counts, and give operators no deterministic way to inspect the excluded rows.
Expose a free-form database query and ask Claude to summarize whichever rows fit the context, without an explicit aggregate or scope contract.

questions.prompt: A security audit asks for counts by actor and day across 100,000 event records, plus a few event IDs for drill-down. The model needs the aggregate, not every raw row. Which tool design is appropriate?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Discovery adds one step for rare requests, but it preserves the long tail while reducing initial context pressure and wrong-tool selection.
details.errorCorrection: Treat tool descriptions as part of the context budget and capability boundary rather than exposing every operation merely because it exists.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A curated initial inventory keeps high-use tool contracts visible while tool search or another controlled discovery mechanism loads detailed rare capabilities only when relevant.
details.scenarioApplication: The assistant can search suppliers, retrieve the selected contract, and summarize it directly; an approved discovery path handles uncommon export or mutation workflows.
details.transfer: For a large tool catalog, measure use and selection quality, keep the narrow high-use surface eager, and discover governed long-tail tools on demand.

messages.text: Loading all definitions recreates the context bloat and leaves similar or rare capabilities competing with the three required tools.
Removing capabilities turns a context problem into an unsupported manual process and loses legitimate procurement workflows.
A universal schema hides distinct contracts behind optional parameters and can increase invalid combinations and selection errors.

feedback.reason: The common workflow needs precise schemas immediately; rare capabilities can be discovered when their governed use is actually selected. This reduces context and selection ambiguity without deleting valid behavior.

options.text: Expose all twenty tools at startup so Claude can choose among every procurement capability without a discovery step.
Keep the three precise read tools available for this workflow and defer rare governed tools to an explicit discovery path.
Remove every tool except a text generator and have procurement staff perform supplier and contract lookups outside the assistant.
Expose only one universal procurement tool with optional parameters so the model sees fewer names while retaining every operation.

questions.prompt: A procurement assistant has twenty available tools, but its current workflow only searches suppliers, retrieves one contract, and summarizes it. Tool descriptions consume much of the initial context. Which configuration is the best first release?

constraints: Tool visibility must follow the validated requesting tenant and user.
High-use authorized reads should be immediate, while rare governed capabilities remain discoverable.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Tenant-scoped discovery adds filtering and invocation checks, yet it retains rare business behavior without exposing unauthorized schemas or actions.
details.errorCorrection: Separate context optimization from authorization: defer capabilities by use, but never let a model-visible catalog grant access.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Tenant and user identity scope the catalog and discovery results, while the server rechecks current permission at invocation before executing a tool.
details.scenarioApplication: Expose the municipality's three core reads, discover regional forms and exports only for that tenant, and reject a stale or cross-tenant request at the server boundary.
details.transfer: In multi-tenant catalogs, curate the eager set by validated access and usage, then enforce the same scope again at execution.

messages.text: A global eager catalog consumes context and exposes irrelevant or unauthorized capability descriptions to every municipality.
Frequency alone is not a reason to delete valid regional behavior; discovery can preserve it without eager context cost.
Prompt wording is not an authorization boundary and can be bypassed by a manipulated or stale request.
Without an eager authorized core, the common path is either bloated with irrelevant tools or lacks its precise read contracts.
Without tenant-scoped discovery and an invocation recheck, rare tools can leak across municipalities or execute after permissions change.

feedback.reason: The common capability surface can be curated per tenant, but rare tools should remain available through controlled discovery. Discovery and execution both need tenant-aware authorization; visibility alone is insufficient.

options.text: Load all 80 definitions for every municipality so the model can discover regional differences from the catalog.
Keep the authorized high-use reads eager and defer rare regional tools so ordinary requests retain their precise contracts without the full catalog.
Delete rare regional tools from the catalog because their low frequency makes their maintenance cost disproportionate.
Show every tool to the model but rely on municipality names in the prompt to prevent cross-tenant calls.
Scope discovery results by validated tenant and user, and recheck the current operation scope at invocation before executing a discovered regional form or export.

questions.prompt: A building-permit platform serves three municipalities through one catalog of 80 tools. Each municipality authorizes a different subset; three core reads dominate, while regional forms and exports are rare. Which TWO configuration decisions preserve capability and authorization? Select TWO.

constraints: The server is currently a local child process connected over stdio.
If the integration changes to HTTP, its HTTP resource authorization requirements apply even to a local listener.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Local process controls require host hardening and careful launch configuration, but they avoid an inapplicable protocol exchange while still protecting the database.
details.errorCorrection: Match the credential and threat control to the actual transport instead of mechanically applying a remote protocol to a local process.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Process ownership, environment permissions, and workstation isolation protect local stdio credentials; an HTTP transport must validate bearer tokens and scopes at its resource boundary, regardless of where the listener runs.
details.scenarioApplication: Keep secrets out of model-visible metadata, restrict the child process environment and files, and apply HTTP authorization when the integration changes from stdio to HTTP.
details.transfer: For integrations, identify who can reach the boundary and choose process, network, or protocol authorization controls accordingly.

messages.text: An HTTP exchange is not the stdio transport boundary and adds no useful resource-server binding inside a local message stream.
Local execution does not eliminate threats from a compromised process, environment, or workstation and cannot justify removing controls.
Secrets in tool descriptions become model-visible metadata and are not a safe credential mechanism.

feedback.reason: The protocol boundary differs by transport. Stdio is protected through the process and environment, while HTTP exposure introduces a resource-server authorization boundary; sensitive data still needs local controls.

options.text: Protect stdio credentials with process, environment, and workstation controls, and apply MCP HTTP authorization requirements whenever the server uses HTTP transport, including a local HTTP listener.
Run a bearer-token exchange through the stdio stream for every local call, even though the child process is not an HTTP resource server.
Assume the local child process is trusted and disable credential checks while the workstation and process environment remain otherwise unrestricted.
Place the local database password in the tool schema so Claude can supply it to the child process when a sensitive query is requested.

questions.prompt: A developer runs a local MCP server as a child process over stdio on a locked workstation. A reviewer proposes applying HTTP bearer-token authorization to every message because the local database is sensitive. Which boundary-specific control is correct?

constraints: The code flow must bind an exact destination and the response to its initiating session.
The client needs protection against authorization-code interception.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The checks require registration and per-request state, but they reduce redirect abuse, response injection, and intercepted-code reuse.
details.errorCorrection: Diagnose authorization as destination, session, and code binding rather than relying on domain ownership or transport confidentiality alone.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Exact URI comparison constrains the redirect, state links the response to the initiating browser transaction, and PKCE binds the authorization code to the verifier held by the client.
details.scenarioApplication: Register the precise callback, generate and validate state per authorization request, and require a code challenge and verifier on the token exchange.
details.transfer: For browser authorization flows, make the redirect exact and bind both the response and code exchange to the initiating client transaction.

messages.text: A domain wildcard still permits an unregistered destination, a fragment does not replace state, and TLS does not bind the code to this client.
Manual copy-paste removes a controlled callback but does not establish a secure redirect or code-binding protocol.
Checking the account after redemption is too late to prevent redirect or authorization-code mix-up.

feedback.reason: A broad redirect accepts destinations the client did not register, missing state allows response mix-up, and missing PKCE leaves a public client code vulnerable to interception. The three controls address distinct bindings.

options.text: Keep a company-domain redirect wildcard, deliver the code through the browser fragment, and rely on TLS and the signed-in account to identify the initiating client.
Remove the callback registration and ask the user to paste the authorization code into the client, treating manual possession as the session binding.
Register one broad callback and compare the account after redemption, without validating a per-request state value or a code verifier.
Require exact pre-registered redirect URIs, validate state for the initiating session, and use PKCE to bind the code exchange to the client.

questions.prompt: A web client starts an MCP authorization flow. The authorization server accepts any redirect URI under the company domain, and the client sends neither state nor PKCE. What should the security diagnosis require?

constraints: Operation visibility should reflect current scopes.
The server must recheck scope and approval before any export or mutation.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Per-user catalogs and invocation checks require refresh and policy plumbing, but they make least privilege visible and enforceable.
details.errorCorrection: Use capability visibility as a convenience and server authorization as the security control; never treat a user request or model plan as a scope grant.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Access-token scopes map to operation permissions; server checks run at invocation so a visible or stale model plan cannot bypass current authorization.
details.scenarioApplication: Expose the read tool for this user, keep export and adjustment unavailable, and reject any attempted call unless the current credential and approval satisfy the operation.
details.transfer: For tool catalogs, filter discovery by scope and reauthorize every consequential call against current identity and policy.

messages.text: Prompt instructions can be bypassed and do not prevent the model from requesting a visible export or adjustment.
Hiding names without server rejection leaves the operation callable and makes a plausible reason an authority substitute.
A model prediction cannot grant a missing scope or provide the approval required for a payroll mutation.

feedback.reason: A logged-in identity alone does not grant every payroll operation. Discovery should reduce accidental exposure, but the resource server remains the authority for current scope and high-impact approval.

options.text: Show read, export, and adjustment tools but add a system instruction that Claude should call export or adjustment only after the user explicitly asks.
Hide export and adjustment in the catalog UI, but let the server accept a hidden call when Claude supplies a business justification in its arguments.
Expose only tools allowed by the current scope, require server-side scope and approval checks for export or adjustment, and reject unauthorized requests.
Grant payroll.export temporarily when a model confidence or task-completion prediction indicates that a payroll file would be useful.

questions.prompt: A payroll tool catalog exposes read, export, and adjustment operations. The user has payroll.read but not payroll.export or payroll.adjust, while the model can still see and request all three. Which enforcement design is correct?

constraints: Authorization may change between discovery and invocation.
The current subject, credential validity, and export scope must be checked at the resource boundary.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A late rejection can waste planning work and require the agent to report an unavailable state, but it prevents execution under revoked authority.
details.errorCorrection: Close the time-of-check/time-of-use gap at invocation instead of trusting an earlier catalog snapshot.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The server validates a current credential, audience, expiry, and operation scope atomically or immediately before the side effect; an audit record explains the rejection.
details.scenarioApplication: Mark the queued handle stale, revalidate or refresh as needed, reject the export after role revocation, and record the attempted operation and subject.
details.transfer: For long-running plans, reauthorize every consequential operation at execution and make revoked or expired capabilities explicit.

messages.text: A cached catalog can outlive role changes and would turn a previously valid plan into an unauthorized export.
Post-production confirmation cannot undo a payroll disclosure and is not an authorization check.
A daily refresh leaves a long revocation window and still trusts stale operation handles.

feedback.reason: Discovery is a capability hint, not a durable grant. Revocation before invocation must take effect at the current resource boundary, before the export is produced.

options.text: Validate the current credential and scope immediately before execution, reject the stale export handle if authorization is gone, and audit the operation and subject.
Trust the discovery result and execute the queued export because the role and token were valid when the agent planned the operation.
Execute the export first and request user confirmation after the payroll file has been generated, so an analyst can cancel future requests.
Refresh the catalog once per day and allow all handles discovered before the refresh to run during the remaining interval.

questions.prompt: A long-running agent discovers a payroll export while the user is authorized, but the role is revoked before the queued invocation reaches the server. What should happen at execution?

constraints: The endpoint now serves six remote clients, bearer tokens, separate tenants, and user sessions.
Process and environment controls protected the old local child process only.
Issuer, audience, expiry, resource, scope, redirect, and invocation checks are available.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the server returns to a local child process with no remote exposure, use process and environment controls again, while keeping application authorization for sensitive operations.
details.errorCorrection: Remote clients are outside the protected process, so environment controls cannot bind a bearer token to its resource, tenant, or scope.
details.mechanismOrProperty: MCP's HTTP authorization requirements differ from stdio, where environment and process controls protect credentials. The scenario's mechanism is governed by this decisive constraint: The transport boundary has changed, so local process controls no longer suffice; remote HTTP authorization and resource-server enforcement are required.
details.scenarioApplication: Use MCP HTTP authorization for the shared endpoint, validate issuer, audience, expiry, resource, and scopes at the resource server, and keep tenant binding and invocation checks independent of model arguments.
details.transfer: Route each information need through the smallest governed interface that matches its evidence shape, and preserve explicit authorization, freshness, and unavailable states when the evidence cannot support a claim.

messages.text: Remote clients are outside the protected process, so environment controls cannot bind a bearer token to its resource, tenant, or scope.
Model-supplied arguments are not an authorization boundary; the resource server must validate the token and enforce tenant and operation scope.
Gateway authentication alone does not establish the resource, tenant, or invocation scope at the resource server for each operation.

feedback.reason: The same logical tools require a different authorization strategy once they cross from local process isolation to a remote shared resource.

options.text: Keep stdio environment controls because the server code and tool names did not change.
Pass the bearer token as a model argument and let the model select the tenant operation before the server executes it.
Terminate tokens at a shared gateway and trust the MCP server to execute any operation named by an authenticated client.
Use MCP HTTP authorization and explicitly validate issuer, audience, expiry, resource, and scopes at the resource server, independent of model arguments.

questions.prompt:
A local MCP server currently runs as a child process over stdio on a locked workstation. The same server is moved behind a shared HTTP endpoint for six remote clients, each with separate tenant scopes and user sessions.

Which authorization design fits the move from local stdio to shared remote HTTP?

constraints: The token expires during generation and the user's role is revoked before the download artifact is released.
The export state is resumable and can be bound to subject, resource, and scope.
The download is consequential and must be audited at completion.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If reauthorization succeeds with the same intended resource and scope, resume from the checkpoint; if it fails, retain the job as unavailable and do not expose the artifact.
details.errorCorrection: The token is expired and the role revoked before a consequential release; discovery-time authority cannot authorize a later artifact.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The resource server must validate that the token is intended for it and must not forward a received token upstream to another resource server. The scenario's mechanism is governed by this decisive constraint: Authorization must be checked at each release boundary; a token valid at discovery cannot authorize a later artifact after expiry or revocation.
details.scenarioApplication: Persist the resumable job, stop release when the token or role is stale, reauthorize and recheck subject, resource, and scope before continuing, and publish only after the current authorization and audit record succeeds.
details.transfer: Route each information need through the smallest governed interface that matches its evidence shape, and preserve explicit authorization, freshness, and unavailable states when the evidence cannot support a claim.

messages.text: Discovery-time authority cannot authorize a later artifact after token expiry and role revocation; logging after delivery is too late.
Starting over loses resumable state and audit continuity; reauthorization should preserve the intended resource and requester linkage.
A role check alone does not revalidate subject, resource, and scope for the artifact; all current authorization fields must pass before release.

feedback.reason: The case integrates token lifecycle with durable workflow state so a safe pause is explicit and resumable.

options.text: Pause release, persist the job, reauthorize, recheck subject, resource, and scope, then publish only with current authorization and audit.
Continue with the original token because its scope was valid when the tool was discovered, then log the expiry after delivery.
Delete the expired job and start a new export under the current session without linking it to the original requester or checkpoint.
Resume after checking only that the current role is present, leaving the original token and resource binding unchanged.

questions.prompt:
A user starts a large payroll export with a valid token. The export job is resumable, but the token expires during generation and the user role is revoked before the download artifact is released.

Which release protocol protects the resumable export after authorization changes?

constraints: The received token must target the current resource and contain the requested scope.
The downstream payroll service is a separate resource server.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Separate validation and credentials add setup and token-management work, but they prevent token confusion and limit the impact of a compromised or overbroad token.
details.errorCorrection: Do not treat transport encryption or model judgment as authorization; bind each token to the resource and operation that will enforce it.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Resource-server validation checks issuer, audience, expiry, and scope; token exchange or another separately issued credential represents the downstream trust relationship.
details.scenarioApplication: Reject a token not intended for the MCP resource, authorize the payroll operation at its scope, and call the downstream service only with its approved credential.
details.transfer: For chained services, validate incoming credentials at every resource boundary and use a least-privileged credential for the next resource.

messages.text: TLS protects transport but does not make a token intended for one resource valid for another or establish the needed scope.
Query parameters expose credentials to logs and do not solve audience or privilege validation.
A model response cannot enforce an authenticated subject, audience, or payroll scope at the resource boundary.

feedback.reason: The MCP server must validate the credential for itself and must not pass a received token to a different resource. A separate downstream credential keeps audiences and least privilege explicit.

options.text: Validate the incoming bearer token only at the MCP edge, then forward it over TLS and let the payroll service decide whether its audience and scopes are acceptable.
Pass the same token in a protected header or query parameter to the downstream service, relying on its normal authentication middleware to reject misuse.
Validate issuer, audience, expiry, and scope at the MCP resource server, then obtain a separately issued least-privileged credential for the downstream resource.
Have Claude decide whether payroll access is appropriate from the request and use the user token for both resources when the explanation is confident.

questions.prompt: An enterprise MCP server exposes payroll over HTTP and forwards a user bearer token to a downstream payroll service without checking audience or scopes. Which authorization design closes the trust boundary?

constraints: Identity and tenant scope must come from validated credentials, not model arguments.
Refund is a high-impact side effect requiring server authorization and an audit trail.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Server authorization and audit logging add latency and operational records, but they prevent tenant crossing and make denied attempts reviewable.
details.errorCorrection: Treat tool parameters as requests to authorize, not as grants of authority, and make the service boundary the enforcement point.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Credential validation supplies identity and tenant context; the resource server checks account ownership and refund permission before its mutation path runs.
details.scenarioApplication: Ignore a model-supplied cross-tenant identity when it conflicts with the token, reject the call, require approval as configured, and audit the denial or mutation.
details.transfer: For any AI-triggered mutation, derive identity server-side, authorize the target resource and action, and retain an auditable decision.

messages.text: Prompt wording cannot bind a model-provided account to the authenticated tenant and leaves the vulnerable backend unchanged.
Model redaction and confidence do not enforce ownership or refund authority at the API boundary.
End-of-day reconciliation is too late to prevent a cross-tenant or duplicate refund and accepts an unauthorized mutation.
Without server-derived identity and resource authorization, an account_id argument can cross tenants or exceed the subject's scope.
Without a pre-mutation approval check and denial audit, a high-impact refund can execute without enforceable authorization or evidence.

feedback.reason: Model arguments are untrusted inputs. The backend must bind resources and side effects to the authenticated subject, enforce the refund scope, and record failures for investigation.

options.text: Keep the model-supplied account_id as the source of tenant identity and add a prompt reminder to use the current account.
Derive the authenticated subject and tenant from validated credentials, authorize the requested account and refund scope at the backend, and reject mismatches.
Let Claude redact suspicious account IDs and approve the refund when its explanation sounds consistent with the user request.
Allow the API to accept any account ID but ask a support analyst to reconcile cross-tenant refunds at the end of the day.
Record denied or mismatched attempts and require the backend to apply the refund approval and least-privilege checks before mutation.

questions.prompt: An expense assistant can call a billing API with model-supplied account_id and refund_amount. The backend trusts those fields, and a test reaches another tenant's account. Which TWO controls must be at the resource boundary? Select TWO.

constraints: The citation verifier depends on the completed draft artifact.
The path must meet a 2.5-second p95 target and at least 95% citation correctness together.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The sequential path is slower, but it protects citation correctness and makes the verifier's input explicit and auditable.
details.errorCorrection: Parallelize only independent work; do not trade away a dependent evidence check for first-order latency without a validated replacement.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Prompt chaining passes one step's output to the next; the application can validate the draft and citations while measuring end-to-end p95 rather than isolated calls.
details.scenarioApplication: Retain the 2.4-second path, record draft and verifier artifacts, and investigate whether precomputed drafts or bounded parallel work can later meet 96% without guessing.
details.transfer: When one stage consumes another's output, preserve the dependency or create a durable equivalent before considering concurrent execution.

messages.text: The observed parallel path already misses the citation floor, and a later reconciliation call is unmeasured and may add latency without restoring evidence.
One prompt hides the draft artifact and removes a separately testable verification boundary; it does not prove the joint quality.
A verifier that infers a missing draft can produce plausible but unsupported citations and still lacks a measured end-to-end contract.

feedback.reason: The verifier has a real dependency on the draft, and the parallel measurement misses the citation floor. Preserve the sequential boundary until an alternative supplies the artifact and clears both gates.

options.text: Keep the sequential prompt chain, pass the draft explicitly to the verifier, and continue validating joint p95 and citation correctness.
Run drafting and verification in parallel and add a reconciliation call later, accepting the observed citation loss while the path is optimized.
Collapse drafting and verification into one prompt so the model can see both tasks without maintaining an intermediate artifact.
Use the faster parallel path and let the verifier infer the missing draft from the source passages it retrieves.

questions.prompt: A claims workflow drafts a recommendation and then verifies its citations. Sequential calls measure 2.4 seconds p95 and 96% citation correctness; parallel calls measure 1.5 seconds and 88% because the verifier lacks the draft. Which boundary should remain?

constraints: Indemnity recall is the decision-relevant quality slice.
Speed and cost must be evaluated jointly with edge-case quality.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Slice evaluation delays a rollout decision, but it avoids scaling either an underperforming model or a blanket rollback that may discard recoverable value.
details.errorCorrection: Do not let an average or one regression dictate a configuration without locating the task slice and measuring the trade-off that matters.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Matched edge cases and end-to-end measurements separate quality failure from transport latency; the team can then test the smallest corrective configuration under the same acceptance criteria.
details.scenarioApplication: Build an indemnity holdout, inspect source coverage and outputs, and compare candidate repairs on recall, p95, cost, and downstream review burden.
details.transfer: When a faster configuration harms a consequential slice, preserve the slice as a gate and test targeted fixes against complete service metrics.

messages.text: The spot check already signals a material indemnity regression; the speed gain does not justify rollout without evaluating this consequential slice.
More output capacity may add cost and tail latency and does not show that missing clauses are caused by generation length.
A rollback may be prudent temporarily, but skipping diagnosis misses whether context or a targeted route could restore quality at lower latency.

feedback.reason: The speed gain is paired with a material decision-quality regression. Slice-level evaluation can show whether the problem is model capability, context, prompt, routing, or an acceptable targeted review path.

options.text: Keep the faster model, monitor indemnity misses after rollout, and treat the current p95 improvement as sufficient evidence while the quality slice remains unmeasured.
Increase the output-token reserve and compare a few longer answers, assuming omitted clauses are a generation-length issue without measuring recall or tail cost.
Compare quality, latency, and cost on indemnity and other edge slices, then choose a prompt/context repair, route, model change, or review path from the evidence.
Restore the former model immediately and postpone a slice evaluation, treating the aggregate regression as proof that the newer configuration has no repairable path.

questions.prompt: A contract analyst replaced a model after aggregate p95 latency fell from 4.2 seconds to 1.4 seconds. Initial dashboards showed aggregate quality; a subsequent spot check found indemnity misses rising from 3% to 11%. What diagnosis should guide the next change?

constraints: The four lookups are independent, but the citation verifier depends on all of them.
The production target is 2.5 seconds p95, with errors and citation correctness measured under load.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Concurrency adds rate-limit and partial-failure handling, but it attacks the measured serialized bottleneck without weakening the citation dependency.
details.errorCorrection: Distinguish average from tail behavior and independent from dependent stages before moving work off the critical path.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Independent calls run concurrently and aggregate programmatically; the dependent verifier consumes the aggregate after a barrier, with concurrency limits protecting the backend.
details.scenarioApplication: Load-test the fanout at production concurrency, record per-call and aggregate failures, and accept the route only if citation quality and p95 satisfy the contract.
details.transfer: Parallelize proven independent calls, keep dependent checks behind an evidence barrier, and validate the complete path under real load.

messages.text: Verification before all lookups can miss the decisive policy clause and make a fast but unsupported citation.
The 3.8-second production tail violates the relevant service behavior even when the average is acceptable.
A fully parallel verifier lacks required evidence, and selecting the fastest result trades correctness for an unvalidated latency number.

feedback.reason: Only the lookup fanout is independent. A bounded concurrent stage can reduce the critical path while the verifier still waits for complete evidence and the service measures its production tail.

options.text: Start the verifier after the first lookup and have it infer the remaining policy evidence, then report the fast path as valid if the average stays below two seconds.
Optimize the 1.6-second average and keep the serialized fan-out, accepting a production p95 above the target because most requests finish sooner.
Run the four independent lookups concurrently with bounded concurrency, aggregate their results, invoke the verifier after the evidence barrier, and load-test p95, errors, and citation correctness.
Run lookup and verification calls concurrently and select the quickest completed verifier result even when it lacks one of the required policy responses.

questions.prompt: A claims request fans out to four independent policy lookups. Average latency is 1.6 seconds, but production p95 reaches 3.8 seconds because the integration serializes the lookups before a dependent citation verifier. Which redesign is justified?

constraints: Retry count and fallback behavior are part of the critical path.
Evidence may be absent when the deadline expires, so the user needs an explicit route or abstention.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Some requests will abstain or reach operations, but the service avoids an unbounded tail and makes missing evidence visible.
details.errorCorrection: Treat retries and fallback as product behavior in the latency and accuracy contract rather than hiding them from measurement.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A deadline and finite retry apply to an idempotent lookup; preserved artifacts can be reused, and an unavailable evidence state prevents the model from presenting unsupported certainty.
details.scenarioApplication: Benchmark one retry and the fallback or abstention path under timeout load, recording p95, citation support, and operations volume.
details.transfer: For retrieval stages, bound recovery, preserve evidence when available, and choose an explicit unavailable state when the correctness budget expires.

messages.text: Two retries already violate the observed tail, and an unvalidated fallback can meet speed by returning unsupported citations.
Removing retrieval abandons the authoritative evidence and does not create a safe answer path merely because it is fast.
Unbounded retries hide failures and measuring only successes gives no valid production tail or availability contract.

feedback.reason: Two retries create the measured tail, while the fallback is unvalidated. A bounded policy makes latency and evidence behavior explicit and evaluates both before rollout.

options.text: Retain both retries for availability, and when they expire return the fallback answer with its ordinary citation field without measuring whether the source supports it.

Set a per-stage deadline with at most one bounded retry for the idempotent lookup, preserve any retrieved artifact, and route or abstain when the evidence budget expires while measuring p95 and citation accuracy.
Remove the retrieval stage when the deadline is tight and let a fast model produce an answer from its trained knowledge, recording the response as a successful low-latency fallback.
Retry until retrieval succeeds and report latency only for successful calls, using the hidden tail as an operational reliability concern rather than a user contract.

questions.prompt: A retrieval tool is usually available within 800 ms, but transient timeouts trigger two full retries; p95 becomes 6.2 seconds and the fallback answer's citation accuracy is unmeasured. Which recovery policy should be tested?

constraints: The ledger cannot parse partial deltas and requires complete validated JSON synchronously within 1 second.
The approved asynchronous contract permits a 1-second acknowledgment and a 4-second complete callback.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The ledger receives its result later and needs callback state, but it never acts on partial or unvalidated JSON.
details.errorCorrection: Design delivery around the consumer's completion semantics, not perceived first-token speed or a deadline renegotiation that the scenario does not permit.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Streaming emits incremental events while SDK accumulation produces a complete message; the ledger contract requires the latter, so asynchronous delivery separates acceptance from validated completion.
details.scenarioApplication: Acknowledge the job, validate JSON and citations, deliver the complete callback by four seconds, and expose callback failure for operations rather than forwarding partial deltas.
details.transfer: When a downstream contract requires complete output, use a supported asynchronous acknowledgment path unless measured final completion fits the synchronous deadline.

messages.text: The ledger cannot parse partial deltas, and early bytes do not produce a complete validated result by its one-second requirement.
A fragment is not a valid complete payload and patching after rejection cannot satisfy the ledger's atomic input contract.
Changing the stated synchronous deadline is not an available design and would still expose a 2.4-second completion to a one-second consumer.

feedback.reason: First-byte latency does not satisfy a consumer that needs one complete validated payload within one second. The supplied asynchronous contract provides the appropriate acknowledgment and completion boundary.

options.text: Use the approved asynchronous contract: acknowledge acceptance within 1 second, then deliver the complete validated JSON by callback within 4 seconds; keep deltas out of the complete-payload parser.
Enable streaming and forward incremental deltas to the ledger, asking its parser to assemble a complete object once enough fields have arrived.
Send the first JSON-looking fragment synchronously and patch missing fields with a later callback if the ledger rejects or cannot parse the fragment.
Increase the synchronous deadline to the measured 2.4 seconds so the final validator can finish, even though the ledger contract specifies one second.

questions.prompt: A policy service emits text deltas after 180 ms, but final validated JSON with a citation check arrives at 2.4 seconds. A claims ledger accepts one complete JSON payload within 1 second and also offers an approved asynchronous contract: acknowledge within 1 second and deliver complete validated JSON by callback within 4 seconds. Which delivery path satisfies the ledger?

constraints: The high-consequence field requires 98% accuracy; the efficient route measures 94% and the stronger route 98.5%.
The stronger route measures 3.4 seconds p95 against a 5-second asynchronous deadline.
A human queue can handle a small unresolved remainder, and cost still requires validation.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the stronger route exceeded the deadline under production load, use a smaller targeted escalation or a reviewed asynchronous workflow rather than accepting 94%.
details.errorCorrection: The held-out result already shows a four-point quality shortfall on a hard field, so waiting for incidents knowingly violates the floor.
details.mechanismOrProperty: For complex accuracy-sensitive work, Anthropic recommends starting capability-first, then evaluating and optimizing efficiency. The scenario's mechanism is governed by this decisive constraint: Quality is the hard constraint for this workload and latency remains feasible, so the efficient-first route must reverse.
details.scenarioApplication: Use the stronger route for the consequence-bearing extraction, validate its end-to-end p95 and cost, and retain a human or explicit unavailable path for unresolved cases.

messages.text: The held-out result already shows a four-point quality shortfall on a hard field, so waiting for incidents knowingly violates the floor.

Which concurrency policy captures the premium value without breaching the global budget?

A quality-based escalation path may be used only after measuring the combined end-to-end behavior.

details.mechanismOrProperty: A workload router can use confidence or a validated slice to invoke the stronger model; the acceptance gate measures both critical-field quality and the full p95 and cost.

details.transfer: Choose the simplest measured configuration that clears the task floor, then test targeted complexity only where its incremental value is demonstrated.

messages.text: The stronger model misses the stated p95 target for every claim, so its accuracy advantage cannot justify a universal default without a new contract.
An extra call can consume the latency budget; its combined p95 and quality effect must be measured rather than inferred from one model call.

feedback.reason: The efficient candidate meets the latency target and has a measured quality baseline; a targeted stronger path may recover hard cases, but its route must be evaluated end to end rather than assumed.

options.text: Use the stronger model for all claims, accepting the 4.8-second p95 as the price of its two-point accuracy gain and revisiting the SLA later.
Use the efficient candidate as the default after holdout validation, then test confidence-based escalation to the stronger model with end-to-end p95, quality, and cost measurement.
Add an unmeasured second validation call to the efficient model and infer that its 2.1-second model time leaves enough room for the full path.

Cost can be optimized after the accepted outcome is measured.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Capability-first evaluation may spend more initially, but it prevents cheap unsupported summaries and makes later savings defensible.
details.errorCorrection: Use the absence of an interactive SLA to optimize efficiency deliberately, not to skip the quality and evidence checks that make the batch useful.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A representative report set evaluates synthesis and citation, while cost and throughput measurements show whether a lower-cost route preserves the accepted outcome.
details.scenarioApplication: Review reports before distribution, compare candidate model or staged paths, and promote a cheaper default only after its citation and synthesis floors hold.
