messages.text: Immediate cheapest selection can distribute unsupported summaries and removes the quality gate that defines batch value.
No interactive SLA does not make quality or spend irrelevant; a permanent strongest model may waste budget without an outcome comparison.
Output coverage is an activity metric and cannot show whether summaries synthesize correctly or cite their sources.
Without a representative quality and citation baseline, cost comparisons cannot show whether a configuration preserves the accepted outcome.
Without a conditional quality gate, a cheaper route can become the default while its summaries or citations fall below the required floor.

feedback.reason: Batch removes an interactive latency constraint but does not remove quality or spend trade-offs. A measured baseline and conditional efficiency test protect the distribution gate.

options.text: Choose the lowest-cost model immediately and treat citation review as an optional editorial step after distribution.
Measure synthesis quality and citation support on representative reports, then compare total spend and throughput for candidate configurations.
Choose the strongest model permanently because batch work has no interactive latency requirement.
Optimize document count processed per night and infer summary quality from whether every report received an output.
Test a lower-cost model or staged route only when its measured summaries and citations continue to meet the accepted outcome floor.

questions.prompt: A research team produces nightly summaries of 500 long scientific reports. There is no interactive latency SLA, but synthesis quality, citation support, and total spend are reviewed before distribution. Which TWO configuration principles fit the batch workload? Select TWO.

constraints: Operational metadata must support latency and tool diagnosis.
Protected content needs minimization, controlled access, and bounded retention.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Some incidents require an approved content sample and may remain partly unresolved, but default logging does not expose protected data unnecessarily.
details.errorCorrection: Treat privacy as a telemetry boundary with explicit sampling and retention, not as a reason to erase the execution graph.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Run and span IDs, timings, configuration, tool names, status, and redacted outcome fields reveal causal behavior; content samples are separately authorized and time-limited.
details.scenarioApplication: Trace a triage run and its tool calls by ID, redact patient fields, restrict any incident sample to approved investigators, and delete it on the defined schedule.
details.transfer: For sensitive AI systems, preserve stage-level operational evidence by default and gate content capture with purpose, access, and retention controls.

messages.text: Indefinite raw capture violates minimization and retention boundaries and creates a larger breach surface than the diagnosis requires.
Suppressing traces removes the timing and tool evidence needed to diagnose production failures.
Model name and count cannot explain a slow span or wrong tool, and memory-based reconstruction is incomplete.

feedback.reason: The default must retain enough signal to locate slow or wrong stages without creating an unrestricted patient transcript. Metadata-first tracing with controlled samples balances diagnosis and minimization.

options.text: Log every patient prompt, retrieved passage, and tool result indefinitely so investigators can reconstruct any run without requesting special access.
Disable tracing by default and retain only monthly uptime and volume, avoiding protected content at the cost of stage-level diagnosis.
Keep correlated metadata and redacted outcomes by default, and capture sampled content only under explicit access, purpose, and retention controls.
Store model name and request count, then ask clinicians to describe the slow or wrong tool run from memory during the incident review.

questions.prompt: A healthcare triage assistant handles protected patient information. Engineers need to understand slow runs and wrong tool calls, but default telemetry must minimize sensitive content. Which telemetry boundary is defensible?

constraints: A successful transport call can still select the wrong tool or evidence.
Existing traces can be compared by version and task outcome.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Trace analysis and a holdout evaluation take time, but they avoid changing unrelated infrastructure and preserve causal attribution.
details.errorCorrection: Separate transport success from task success and use the execution evidence already captured to diagnose the changed configuration.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Join prompt/tool versions to selected operation, parameters, evidence, and outcome labels; compare matched cases to locate the changed decision boundary.
details.scenarioApplication: Build a release comparison for tool selection accuracy, valid parameters, retrieval support, and answer correctness, then test a targeted description repair.
details.transfer: When quality changes without availability changes, compare versioned execution paths and outcome labels before treating the issue as capacity.

messages.text: A broad rollback confounds the tool-description change with unrelated infrastructure and cannot explain which path recovered.
More output capacity does not test tool selection or retrieval evidence and may increase cost without addressing the changed contract.
Transport success can mask a wrong tool or unsupported answer, so API error rate is not a task-quality diagnosis.

feedback.reason: The changed description can alter tool selection or arguments without affecting transport health. Versioned traces and task outcomes can isolate that path before a broad rollback or tuning change.

options.text: Roll back the tool description and every related infrastructure change, then attribute recovery to the description because it was the most recent release.
Compare versioned traces and evaluation outcomes for tool selection, parameters, retrieval evidence, and answer correctness before changing infrastructure.
Raise output-token limits and retry completed calls, assuming unchanged uptime means the model needs more generation capacity rather than a different tool path.
Compare only API error rates by release, treating any request that returned HTTP success as correct for the policy task.

questions.prompt: A policy assistant's accuracy drops after a tool-description revision, while uptime and average latency remain unchanged. Request IDs, tool-call spans, and prompt versions exist, but there is no comparison dashboard. What diagnosis should come first?

constraints: Sampling must retain rare failures and tail-latency evidence.
Sensitive payloads must not become an unrestricted default log.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Triggered streams add collector and storage rules, but they provide evidence for rare incidents without logging all successful conversations.
details.errorCorrection: Design sampling around failure and tail observability, not only volume, and keep content handling separate from event selection.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The collector samples error and latency thresholds separately from ordinary traffic, labels tool and version, and applies access and retention policy to any content fields.
details.scenarioApplication: Retain denied-call metadata and span timing at high recall, sample authorized payloads only when approved, and measure whether the design captures the incident class.
details.transfer: For low-rate failures, stratify by error and latency, bound retention, and verify that the sample captures the class needed for diagnosis.

messages.text: Successful head samples cannot explain a failure class they never capture, regardless of how predictable the sample rate is.
Capturing complete conversations can preserve the rare event, but broadly retaining their sensitive payloads exceeds the metadata and controlled samples needed for this diagnosis.
Increasing uniform sampling may still miss 0.1% events and does not guarantee retention of the tail or protect sensitive content.

feedback.reason: Uniform head sampling is demonstrably missing the rare class. Triggered sampling can preserve failure and tail evidence while metadata redaction and retention bounds keep privacy exposure controlled.

options.text: Keep uniform head sampling at one percent and infer denied-call behavior from successful traffic because the rate and collector configuration are stable.
Capture complete conversations for a fixed extended retention period so the rare failure class is unlikely to be missed, without creating a separate error-triggered sampling stratum.
Use error- and latency-triggered sampling with bounded retention, stratified metadata by tool and version, and redacted or access-controlled sensitive fields.
Increase uniform head sampling until the expected failure count is statistically visible, but keep the same payload retention and no error-triggered stratum.

questions.prompt: A low-rate tool authorization failure affects 0.1% of requests, while 1% head sampling captures only successful traffic. Operators cannot explain denied calls or their latency tails. Which sampling design should be tested?

constraints: Each child execution and retry must remain joinable to the lead run.
The report completeness outcome must link to the causal execution path without raw research content.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Identifier propagation and trace joins add schema and queue plumbing, but they turn an intermittent missing section into an inspectable execution path.
details.errorCorrection: Preserve causal identity across asynchronous boundaries rather than relying on independent logs or aggregate queue health.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Queue metadata carries a parent and child span identity; the trace store joins worker outcomes and evidence handles to the lead synthesis and completeness result.
details.scenarioApplication: Create a child span for every worker and retry, attach retrieval IDs and status, and mark which report section consumed each artifact.
details.transfer: For queued or parallel agents, carry parent-child trace context and connect evidence and final outcomes while keeping sensitive content governed separately.

messages.text: Manual log inspection and queue depth cannot prove which worker or retrieval artifact caused a specific report gap.
Final output and queue depth lack the child path needed for diagnosis; identifiers themselves need not contain research content.
Independent IDs without a propagated parent link make it impossible to relate a retry to the lead run; retries should use child spans under the same trace.

feedback.reason: Local IDs cannot establish parent-child causality. Propagating a run ID and recording structured child, evidence, and retry links lets operators trace the missing section without storing the research text itself.

options.text: Propagate the parent run identifier through queue messages, emit structured child spans and evidence links, and join them to the report-completeness result in the trace store.
Inspect workers' independent logs manually and compare queue depth with the final report whenever a user reports a missing section.
Store only the final report and aggregate queue depth, reasoning that child identifiers would expose research content and are unnecessary for diagnosis.
Assign a fresh trace ID to each retry and aggregate the IDs after synthesis, preserving local isolation while losing the original parent-child chain.

questions.prompt: A lead agent launches asynchronous workers through a queue. Worker logs contain local request IDs, but the final report cannot identify which worker, retrieval result, or retry caused a missing section. What trace change is needed?

constraints: The privacy officer authorizes one reviewer and a 30-minute review with specified request IDs and redaction.

details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic emphasizes high-level patterns that provide operational signal without exposing conversation contents when privacy matters. options.text: Keep telemetry metadata-only even during the authorized review because content must never enter observability.

options.text: Join traces to outcome IDs, compare prompt/retrieval versions, and target rollback or repair to the component explaining the loss.

constraints: Operators need causal evidence across retrieval, model, and tool stages.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Structured tracing and sampling require schema and storage discipline, but they make high-volume failures reproducible without building an unrestricted transcript lake.

details.mechanismOrProperty: A trace ID links the run and child spans; metadata, versions, timings, resource use, and outcome classifications diagnose execution without requiring every protected payload by default.

messages.text: Rerunning later may use different data or configuration and still cannot show which stage failed in the original execution.
A broad raw archive, even with fixed retention, increases privacy and search exposure and does not provide structured causal spans for retrieval, model, or tool diagnosis.

options.text: Store the final answer and availability, then rerun the same question during an incident and compare the later response with the operator's memory of the failure.

Record model version, request count, and monthly uptime, and ask service owners to add detail only when a repeated incident becomes severe.
Emit correlated structured traces for configuration, retrieval, model and tool spans, resource use, failure class, and outcome, with privacy-aware content handling.

details.scenarioApplication: Track start/end/status and evidence counts per worker and tool, join them to the synthesis and completeness result, and alert on p95 or branch failure classes.

messages.text: Report length and daily averages cannot identify a slow or failed branch or distinguish a concise complete report from an incomplete one.

Without per-step correlated timing and status, intermittent tail behavior cannot be localized to a worker, tool, or release.
Without outcome links, telemetry cannot show which branch or evidence path caused the incomplete report.

feedback.reason: Tail latency and incomplete reports require both per-branch execution timing and an outcome join. Averages or report length alone hide the failed branch; raw transcripts add privacy risk without causal structure.

options.text: Track only final report length and daily average latency so the monitoring dashboard stays simple.
Emit correlated per-step timing and status for each worker, tool, retrieval, and synthesis span, segmented by deployment version.
Keep permanent unrestricted copies of all conversations so analysts can search for any missing section later.
Alert on the mean latency and sample a single worker log whenever the daily average changes.
Record worker, evidence, synthesis, and report-completeness outcomes so a missing section can be traced to a branch and release.

questions.prompt: A research workflow runs several agents and tools in parallel. Average latency is acceptable, but p95 spikes intermittently and users report incomplete reports. Which TWO telemetry priorities are most useful? Select TWO.

constraints: The full authoritative corpus fits the target context with room for the question and response.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Full context may consume more tokens than selective retrieval, but it reduces indexing and ranking failure modes while the corpus fits.
details.errorCorrection: Choose RAG for a measured information-shape or scale problem rather than assuming every knowledge base needs vectors.

details.scenarioApplication: Load the corpus with document boundaries, put the changing question after it, and monitor context and latency before adding chunking and ranking infrastructure.
details.transfer: Start with the simplest authoritative context design that fits the workload, then introduce retrieval when corpus growth or relevance evidence justifies it.

messages.text: Immediate indexing and reranking add operational complexity without a demonstrated context or relevance problem.
A retrieval layer and coarse topic chunks add indexing and ranking failure modes before the corpus needs selective access; they do not improve the already fitting full-context path.

feedback.reason: The corpus fits and is required broadly, so a structured full-context path is simpler and more authoritative than an unneeded retrieval layer. RAG can be introduced when measured size, latency, or query needs require it.

options.text: Build vectors and a reranker immediately so the changing question can select a smaller context, even though the full authoritative corpus currently fits.
Provide the structured full corpus, place the variable question after it, cache the stable prefix where useful, and introduce RAG only when growth or context limits are measured.
Build a vector index with coarse topic chunks and rerank every question to reduce prompt size, even though the full authoritative corpus currently fits with room for the query.
Create a small extractive summary of the corpus for each request and link analysts to full sections only when they dispute an answer.

questions.prompt: A laboratory has a stable authoritative corpus of 90,000 tokens used for broad questions by a small analyst group. It fits the selected context window, and the changing question can follow the source. Which first-release boundary is proportionate?

constraints: A numeric answer needs the table labels and units in its evidence chunk.
The retrieval location is correct; the source-to-chunk transformation is the suspected fault.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Richer chunks increase index size and may reduce granularity, so evaluate them on numeric recall, citation support, and retrieval cost.
details.errorCorrection: Repair the evidence representation when the source-to-chunk boundary loses semantics; do not mask it with broader retrieval or inference.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Contextualized structure gives retrieval and generation the relationships needed to interpret a numeric row; reindexing and source comparison test whether the repair restores accuracy.
details.scenarioApplication: Include table and section identifiers in each chunk, run torque holdouts with units, and reject answers whose evidence span does not support the numeric value.
details.transfer: When RAG finds the right location but the answer is wrong, inspect chunk structure and contextual labels before changing embeddings or model behavior.

messages.text: More vectors and top-K do not restore the missing heading or unit and can increase distractors while encouraging an inferred value.
A full manual raises context cost and hides the evidence boundary; it is not a targeted repair for a lost table label.
Plausibility is not source support, and accepting inferred units can propagate a silent numeric error.

feedback.reason: The correct section cannot compensate for lost table semantics. Restoring heading, labels, units, and context in the chunk addresses the observed transformation defect before changing ranking.

options.text: Rebuild the chunk with its table heading, column labels, units, nearby procedure context, and section ID, then reindex and evaluate numeric answers against the source.
Increase embedding size and top-K, leave the isolated table row unchanged, and let generation select a plausible unit from nearby retrieved engineering passages.
Place the full manual in every request so Claude can infer the missing heading and unit from surrounding pages instead of changing the index.
Accept a numeric unit when it falls within a familiar engineering range and send only unusually large deviations to a reviewer.

questions.prompt: After an equipment-manual migration, retrieval finds the correct section, but answers misstate a torque value because a table row was indexed without its column heading and unit. What should be repaired first?

constraints: Boundary-case answers need adjacent exception context.
The index should retain retrieval granularity rather than making every chunk a full manual.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Overlap increases index and prompt cost and can introduce duplicate passages, so use the smallest measured expansion that restores exception recall.
details.errorCorrection: Repair the chunk boundary and context expansion before relying on model inference or unbounded candidate counts.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Section-aware chunking can include the next section or parent context when a cross-reference is detected; evaluation checks whether the exception and citation arrive together.
details.scenarioApplication: Build boundary-case queries, compare fixed and overlap variants, and retain section IDs and neighboring references in the evidence returned to Claude.
details.transfer: For manuals and policies with cross-references, test structure-aware chunks and controlled neighboring context against boundary-case evidence.

messages.text: General knowledge cannot safely supply a missing safety exception and hides the evidence gap.
Whole-manual chunks destroy retrieval granularity and inflate context for ordinary questions.
More candidates may add the next section but does not guarantee adjacency or prevent irrelevant clauses from crowding the answer.

feedback.reason: The failure is a chunk boundary that separates an exception from its governing rule. Controlled overlap or parent expansion restores adjacent scope while preserving meaningful retrieval units and makes the trade-off measurable.

options.text: Keep fixed windows and ask Claude to infer an omitted exception from general safety knowledge when a boundary case is detected.
Make each chunk the complete manual so every cross-reference is present, accepting a large context and losing section-level retrieval precision.
Use section-aware chunks with controlled overlap or parent-context expansion, then compare boundary recall and citation completeness with fixed chunks while tracking index and prompt cost.
Increase top-K until both sections appear, without changing boundaries or testing whether the extra sections introduce unrelated rules.

questions.prompt: A safety manual contains cross-references where an exception starts in one section and its scope continues into the next. Fixed 300-token chunks retrieve the rule but omit the exception on boundary cases. Which chunking change should be tested?

constraints: Deleted revision content must not answer current queries.
Retrieval and citation tests must enforce tenant and active-revision state.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Deletion propagation and tombstone checks add operational complexity and may reduce recall, but they protect retention obligations and citation correctness.
details.errorCorrection: Enforce content lifecycle and authority before generation rather than relying on ranking, recency, or prompt admonitions.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The index lifecycle marks vectors unavailable and the retriever applies tenant and revision filters before evidence is returned; the model is not asked to enforce deletion from mixed chunks.
details.scenarioApplication: Process the R2 deletion event, verify no active query retrieves it, index R3 with its version, and test citations against current and historical modes separately.
details.transfer: For mutable corpora, treat deletion and version filters as retrieval invariants and test them at ingestion, index, query, and citation boundaries.

messages.text: Claude cannot reliably enforce deletion or revision policy when stale and current chunks are both available.
A score preference does not remove deleted content and can still return R2 when the query matches it better.
A prompt note is not an index authorization or retention control and leaves the deleted clause searchable.

feedback.reason: Retention and revision state are index and retrieval responsibilities. Tombstoning or removing R2 and filtering active revisions prevents stale evidence from reaching generation; tests prove the deletion boundary.

options.text: Mark R2 unavailable, remove or tombstone its vectors, filter retrieval to the tenant's active revisions, and run deletion and citation tests before exposing R3.

questions.prompt: A code-review agent repairs a vulnerable authentication handler in an isolated repository, and valid implementations may use different tool sequences. Select TWO grading controls.

constraints: The task and grader disagree about the required path.

details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends a known working reference solution to verify task and grader configuration; provenance, deduplication, and holdout separation are scenario controls.

Request IDs correlate provider evidence with application traces.
A global timeout or model change would mask the affected stage.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If every region had the same p99 and only one model version regressed across routes, a global rollback would become a stronger next action.
details.errorCorrection: A global timeout, global model change, or monthly cost view changes or observes the wrong dimension and cannot locate the latency cause.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic includes a unique request ID in responses and errors so operators can correlate a failing request with application traces and support investigations.
details.scenarioApplication: Compute regional p95/p99, split by model and cache state, join request IDs to stage spans, and contain only the implicated path.
details.transfer: Diagnose tail and segment behavior with correlated request evidence before changing a shared service setting.

messages.text: A larger timeout masks failures and does not identify the regional stage.
A global model change removes the useful regional comparison.
Cost reporting lacks the request and stage timing needed for diagnosis.

feedback.reason: A localized timeout can be hidden by a stable global average; segment and tail analysis with correlated traces identifies the failing stage before intervention.

options.text: Raise the global timeout so the region’s user-visible failures are less frequent.
Switch every region to a larger model and compare regional and global average latency after rollout.
Inspect the monthly cost report for evidence of the regional timeout.
Slice regional p95/p99 by model, context, and cache; correlate request IDs with stage timings.

questions.prompt: Average latency is stable while one region reports timeouts. Request IDs, model/workspace, context and cache fields, region, and per-stage timings are retained. What should the operator inspect first?

constraints: Redacted samples and outcome labels can link to request traces.
The new document slice is distinguishable.
Governed sampling and a quality trigger are available.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the new type had no user-facing quality requirement and only provider capacity mattered, usage and latency could be sufficient operational signals.
details.errorCorrection: Provider panels omit task grounding, indefinite retention violates governance, and removing the slice hides rather than measures the regression.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends combining automated evaluations with production monitoring, feedback, A/B tests, and transcript review for a holistic view.
details.scenarioApplication: Use redacted traces and labels to quantify the document slice, add representative cases to evaluation, and alert the quality owner without broad raw retention.
details.transfer: Keep provider health and user outcome quality as separate signals, and route governed production samples back into evaluation.

messages.text: Provider infrastructure metrics cannot detect a content-grounding regression.
Provider usage, latency, and error panels cannot reveal a grounded-answer regression in the new document slice.
Removing the slice hides the quality behavior instead of diagnosing it.

feedback.reason: Infrastructure health does not establish grounded answer quality; the new slice needs governed evidence and a repeatable evaluation response.

options.text: Declare the release healthy because provider usage, latency, and errors are green.
Route reviewer complaints to provider usage dashboards and wait for a larger sample while infrastructure health remains green.
Remove the new document type from the product until provider dashboards show a quality signal.
Investigate the quality slice with governed samples, add regression cases, and separate task quality from provider health.

questions.prompt: Provider usage, latency, and error dashboards remain green, but sampled reviewers report a sharp drop in grounded answers for a newly introduced document type. Raw conversations cannot be retained broadly. What should the team do?

constraints: Exporter heartbeat and last-sample time are available.
Gateway request counts can distinguish a stale series from a genuine zero.
The alert must carry scope, freshness, evidence, owner, and next action.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If heartbeat, gateway, application, and quality counts all reconciled for the interval, the dashboard could remain quiet without an unknown-health alert.
details.errorCorrection: Current provider panels do not prove missing regional application or quality telemetry, suppressing alerts hides uncertainty, and an ownerless page lacks actionable scope.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic distinguishes production monitoring from evaluation and review: live monitoring can reveal behavior but can also lack grading ground truth; freshness and ownership are scenario controls.
details.scenarioApplication: Use the heartbeat and request-count mismatch to mark eu-west unknown, page the telemetry owner, and escalate to the service owner when the gap cannot be repaired promptly.
details.transfer: Treat stale or missing telemetry as an explicit unknown state and make alerts carry enough scope and evidence for the named owner to act.

messages.text: Provider spend and errors do not establish the health of missing regional application spans.
Suppressing quality alerts converts an evidence gap into a false green state.
A current exporter heartbeat proves data flow, not that application spans and quality outcomes reconcile for the affected requests.

feedback.reason: Missing telemetry cannot establish service health; the response should make the unknown interval visible, route it to the telemetry owner, and preserve a service investigation path.

options.text: Mark eu-west unknown, page telemetry owner with stale/request evidence, and escalate service if the gap persists.
Keep the dashboard green because provider spend and error panels are current.
Suppress quality alerts until the exporter returns and close the event as infrastructure-only, then review next shift.
Restore the exporter and, once its heartbeat is current, treat the regional dashboard as healthy without reconciling application spans or quality labels.

questions.prompt: An overnight dashboard shows zero errors and normal spend, but the eu-west telemetry exporter stopped sending data 42 minutes ago. The load balancer records 15,000 requests there, while application spans and quality labels are absent. The runbook has telemetry and service owners. What should the on-call do?

constraints: Provider usage dimensions, gateway route logs, request traces from healthy routes, and the affected case set are available; cached and uncached input are reported only at provider aggregation level.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If every route preserved a stable case/request key and the Usage API dimensions reconciled to the application ledger, aggregate usage could be used with the existing slice dashboards.
details.errorCorrection: Average allocation hides route-specific retries, cache state, and case mix, so it cannot explain the quality regression or support a cost-per-outcome decision. The competing action therefore leaves the stated decision boundary unresolved.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic's Usage API reports token consumption with filters and grouping by dimensions such as model and workspace, including cached and uncached input. The case-specific population, thresholds, roles, and authority limits are supplied by this scenario rather than by the provider documentation.
details.scenarioApplication: Repair the gateway trace key and reconcile provider usage to application cases for the affected route, report unattributed usage separately, and investigate quality using the joined traces and reviewed cases.
details.transfer: Join provider measurements to the application unit of work before attributing cost or quality to a route.

messages.text: Averages hide route-specific retries, cache state, and case mix, so they cannot explain the affected class.
Normal aggregate spend does not connect the model to the reported cases or prove a model cause.
Healthy-route estimates do not establish the affected route’s cost, quality, or service boundary.

feedback.reason: Repair the gateway trace key and reconcile provider usage to application cases for the affected route, report unattributed usage separately, and investigate quality using the joined traces and reviewed cases. The decisive constraint is Provider totals can account for spend but cannot attribute a quality regression to cases without an application-level join; missing joins must remain explicitly unknown rather than inferred from aggregate spend.

options.text: Divide workspace token totals by the number of cases and estimate the affected class from the aggregate dashboard.
Attribute the quality regression to the model because workspace token totals remain normal.
Repair the gateway trace key, join provider usage to cases, separate unattributed usage, and investigate quality with reviewed traces.
Estimate a cost per case from the healthy routes and change the affected workflow SLA immediately.

questions.prompt: The Usage API reports normal hourly tokens by workspace and model, but the application cannot map those totals to case IDs because one gateway route drops the trace key. A quality regression is reported for one workflow class. What should the team repair first?

constraints: Workspace boundaries are established.
Provider-aligned usage dimensions are required for provider accounting; application capacity and request attribution are separate measures.
Raw prompt storage is restricted.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the requirement were only application latency and capacity diagnosis with no provider accounting, gateway traces could be primary and Usage API records secondary.
details.errorCorrection: Character estimates and monthly invoices cannot provide the required provider dimensions or hourly view; provider totals alone do not prove application capacity or per-request cost; storing prompts violates the data boundary.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic's Usage API reports token consumption with filters and grouping by dimensions such as model and workspace, including cached and uncached input. The scenario policy keeps capacity telemetry and the approved cost ledger as separate application measures.
details.scenarioApplication: Anchor provider accounting in Usage API records with model, workspace, and cache dimensions; join approved request metadata to gateway capacity and cost records, and flag unjoined attribution for follow-up.
details.transfer: Use provider-reported dimensions for provider accounting, then join explicitly owned application telemetry for operational measures without storing sensitive request content.

messages.text: Character conversion and delayed invoices lose provider cache and workspace dimensions and cannot support reliable hourly attribution.
Provider totals establish usage dimensions but cannot by themselves establish capacity or a per-request cost when no application join exists.
Full prompts create unnecessary sensitive storage and still do not make local reconstruction the provider accounting authority.

feedback.reason: The Usage API supplies provider token dimensions, while capacity and per-request attribution require application joins; missing joins must remain unknown rather than being replaced by estimates or prompt storage.

options.text: Use application character counts plus monthly invoices as the ledger, then derive hourly token, capacity, and spend alerts from estimated totals and workspace averages.
Use Usage API records grouped by model, workspace, and cache state for provider token accounting, then join request metadata to gateway capacity and approved cost records.
Use provider usage totals alone for per-request cost and capacity alerts, treating an unjoined record as a workspace-average request and continuing the dashboard.
Store complete prompts as the authoritative ledger, reconstruct tokens and costs locally, and treat provider reports as monthly reconciliation for capacity and billing.

questions.prompt: An organization needs hourly and daily token trends by model and workspace, cached versus uncached input, cost attribution, capacity signals, and alerts across environments. Which data source should anchor accounting?

constraints: Provider error types and retry-after are available.
Usage and cost can be grouped by workspace.
Spend-cap failures remain failing until access resumes.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the provider documented every failure as transient with retry-after and the gateway had no spend-cap path, bounded exponential backoff could be the only recovery branch.
details.errorCorrection: Daily aggregation can miss a burst or rate-limit event; a shared backoff path cannot clear a persistent spend cap; and increasing retries without classification amplifies cost and traffic.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic documents distinct error types, retry-after semantics, exponential backoff for transient failures, and a separate spend-cap condition that keeps failing until access resumes. Burst thresholds, alert ownership, and routing are scenario policy.
details.scenarioApplication: Classify each response, apply retry-after and bounded exponential backoff only to documented transient conditions, emit separate workspace signals for burst or rate-limit utilization, spend exhaustion, and repeated failures, and route each threshold breach to its owner.
details.transfer: Pair each provider failure class with a bounded action and owner, and keep rate-limit, repeated-failure, and spend-cap monitoring distinct enough to change the response.

messages.text: Daily aggregation can miss a burst or rate-limit event even though the retry treatment and spend alert are sound; the gateway needs a timely utilization warning.
Immediate burst monitoring and spend routing are useful, but persistent spend caps must not share a retry path with transient errors.
Being near a spend cap does not establish exhausted access; increasing retries before classifying the error can amplify rate and spend instead of choosing the documented response.

feedback.reason: The documented error classes determine retry eligibility, while the scenario requires separate burst, spend, and repeated-failure signals with an owner action; a spend cap remains failing and must be routed rather than retried.

options.text: Classify errors, honor retry-after with bounded backoff for transient cases, and alert workspace spend exhaustion, but aggregate burst/rate-limit utilization only in a daily report.
Alert burst/rate-limit utilization immediately and route workspace spend exhaustion to its owner, but use the same configured backoff path for transient and persistent spend-cap failures.

Monitor burst/rate-limit utilization, workspace spend, and repeated failures separately; use retry-after with bounded backoff only for transient errors, and route threshold breaches or spend caps to named owners.
Monitor burst/rate-limit utilization, workspace spend, and repeated failures, route alerts to an owner, but increase retries as a workspace nears its spend cap before classifying the error.

questions.prompt: A shared API gateway must warn on burst traffic, workspace spend exhaustion, and repeated provider failures while retrying only recoverable conditions. What monitoring and response policy fits?

constraints: Payment authority can be narrow and policy-checked.
Untrusted content can be screened and red-team cases can run in the harness.
The assistant’s payment draft is reversible until submission.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the assistant only produced a reversible draft with no payment capability, confirmation could move to the later application action.
details.errorCorrection: Broad authority, obscurity, and after-the-fact review rely on probabilistic behavior or leave an irreversible path open.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends layering input and tool-output screening, hardened instructions, confirmation, least privilege, red-teaming, and continuous monitoring.
details.scenarioApplication: Bind confirmation to the proposed payment, enforce policy at the tool, test injected content, and monitor attempted and completed payment actions.
details.transfer: Layer prevention, authorization, and detection at a consequential side-effect boundary.

messages.text: A prompt cannot reliably constrain an irreversible tool when credentials are broad.
Hiding an endpoint removes evidence but does not authorize or prevent a call.
Automatic low-value writes still create an unaudited side effect and may be cumulative.
Exact confirmation and a policy-checked narrow action make the approved side effect explicit.
Screening, red-teaming, monitoring, and least privilege provide independent defenses against bypass and blast radius.

feedback.reason: Exact confirmation and application authorization prevent an unaudited write, while layered screening, testing, monitoring, and least privilege reduce bypass and blast radius.

options.text: Require explicit human confirmation for the exact payment and enforce a narrow policy-checked payment action.
Grant broad payment authority and depend on a friendly system prompt to prevent injected calls.
Hide the payment endpoint from logs so an attacker cannot learn how the tool works.
Let the assistant submit low-value payments automatically and review only exceptions afterward.
Screen untrusted inputs and tool outputs, red-team bypasses, monitor the workflow, and keep payment credentials least-privileged.

questions.prompt: A treasury assistant proposes vendor payments, but prompt injection could trigger an unaudited external payment. Select TWO controls that protect the side-effect boundary.

constraints: The attack enters through OCR from an untrusted document.
Classification does not require a payment write.
The team can rerun injection tests in the real harness.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If OCR were from a trusted internal source and the classifier had no side-effect tools, prompt construction would be a lower-risk quality concern.
details.errorCorrection: A warning or prompt rewrite leaves an untrusted message construction path; removing only write access still allows content injection to affect classification.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic distinguishes indirect injection in documents and tool results and recommends structured untrusted results, output screening, and narrow permissions.
details.scenarioApplication: Represent OCR as untrusted tool output, screen it, give the classifier only needed read and classify tools, and test hostile OCR through the deployment-shaped harness.
details.transfer: When a failure combines content confusion with excessive authority, repair both trust and privilege boundaries before tuning behavior.

messages.text: A warning does not restore the data boundary or remove the payment side effect.
Removing write access leaves the indirect injection path and can still corrupt classification.
Prompt wording cannot replace structured untrusted data or least-privilege enforcement.

feedback.reason: The incident has two independent causes: the data trust boundary is lost and classification has unnecessary high-impact authority. Both must be closed before prompt tuning.

options.text: Keep OCR as user text, add a stronger warning, and monitor payment calls for suspicious content.
Remove payment access but leave OCR concatenated with user instructions so classification can keep its current prompt.
Keep OCR untrusted, screen it, remove payment write from the classifier, and rerun injection tests.
Rewrite the classifier prompt, keep payment authority, and add a post-call monitor for suspicious transfers.

questions.prompt: An accounts-payable classifier follows malicious OCR text and attempts a payment-tool call; OCR was concatenated into an ordinary user message and the agent has payment write access. What should be fixed first?

constraints: A proxy records arbitrary destinations and query strings.
An egress allowlist and URL policy are available.
A canary secret can test whether fetched content leaves through the proxy.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: With an offline local corpus and no network-capable tool, URL filtering would be unnecessary and content isolation would address the remaining injection risk.
details.errorCorrection: Read-only source access does not remove the network side channel, unrestricted debugging expands it, and blocking all research abandons the stated task.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends isolating third-party content in tool results, screening tool outputs, and limiting sensitive data and actions with least privilege; the proxy and canary are scenario controls.
details.scenarioApplication: Allow only approved destinations and URL shapes, remove unnecessary secrets from model context, and verify that a canary cannot be encoded into outbound query or image URLs.
details.transfer: Model network output as a side-effect channel and control destinations, payload shape, and sensitive context separately from write permissions.

messages.text: Approved domains do not prevent a malicious page from encoding case text in a query or image URL; post-request review is late.
Context sanitization addresses prompt content but leaves the proxy as an unrestricted data-egress channel.
A domain allowlist narrows destinations, but arbitrary query strings and no canary leave exfiltration untested.

feedback.reason: A read-only tool can still transmit data through an allowed network request, so egress and sensitive-context controls are independent of source mutation authority.

options.text: Allow approved research domains with arbitrary URL and query construction, relying on proxy alerts or periodic review after requests.
Sanitize fetched text before context insertion while leaving outbound destinations and query strings unrestricted for research coverage.
Use a fixed domain allowlist but permit arbitrary query strings and omit canary testing to keep the research path lightweight.
Keep content untrusted, allowlist egress and URL/query shapes, minimize secrets, and test URL exfiltration with a canary.

questions.prompt: A research agent has only a read-only HTTP fetch tool, yet a malicious page instructs it to place case text in an image URL. The team assumes no write tool means no meaningful side effect. Which control is needed?

constraints: The screening dependency status, untrusted invoice, draft parameters, confirmation state, and side-effect action are recorded; the payment tool is otherwise available.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If screening were advisory, the action had no external effect, and the policy owner explicitly accepted that degraded mode, a documented unavailable state could be advisory rather than a hard hold.
details.errorCorrection: The state may have changed after screening and the scenario defines screening as a required control; bypassing it turns an availability failure into an unobserved side effect. The competing action therefore leaves the stated decision boundary unresolved.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends layering input and tool-output screening, hardened instructions, confirmation, least privilege, red-teaming, and continuous monitoring. The case-specific population, thresholds, roles, and authority limits are supplied by this scenario rather than by the provider documentation.
details.scenarioApplication: Hold or quarantine the draft, emit an explicit dependency-unavailable state, notify the payment owner, and submit only after screening and confirmation are revalidated.
details.transfer: Fail closed at a consequential side effect when a required safety layer is unavailable, and expose the unavailable state.

messages.text: The required screen may no longer represent the current state, so confirmation alone does not restore the safety layer.
A low-value exception still creates an unobserved side effect when the scenario defines screening as required.
A second confirmation does not revalidate the unavailable dependency or its evidence.

feedback.reason: Hold or quarantine the draft, emit an explicit dependency-unavailable state, notify the payment owner, and submit only after screening and confirmation are revalidated. The decisive constraint is A required safety layer is unavailable at the side-effect boundary, so the workflow must fail closed even though the content was screened earlier and a confirmation is pending.

options.text: Submit after the existing confirmation because the invoice was screened before the outage.
Hold the draft, emit dependency-unavailable, notify the owner, and revalidate screening and confirmation before submission.
Bypass screening for low-value payments and keep the normal confirmation step.
Treat the earlier screen as valid until recovery and submit whenever the requester confirms again.

questions.prompt: A payment assistant has correctly screened an untrusted invoice and prepared a narrow draft, but the screening service becomes unavailable immediately before the payment action. The draft is still awaiting accountable confirmation. What should happen at the unavailable safety boundary?

constraints: The screen result, OCR fixture, prior false-positive rate, invoice provenance, tool permissions, and reviewer identity are available; no payment has been submitted.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the screen had a validated benign result, stable false-positive behavior, and the normal confirmation path, the payment could proceed under the existing layered side-effect control.
details.errorCorrection: Global threshold changes can admit hostile content, while ignoring an unexplained signal removes the safety boundary without evidence that the benign case is safe. The competing action therefore leaves the stated decision boundary unresolved.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends layering input and tool-output screening, hardened instructions, confirmation, least privilege, red-teaming, and continuous monitoring. The case-specific population, thresholds, roles, and authority limits are supplied by this scenario rather than by the provider documentation.
details.scenarioApplication: Keep the invoice quarantined, show the reviewer the flagged span and uncertainty, run the approved false-positive/benign fixture checks, and recalibrate or route the screen for review before any payment action.
details.transfer: Make uncertainty visible and calibrate a safety signal with representative positive and negative cases before releasing a side effect.

messages.text: A global threshold change can admit hostile content and is not calibrated to this false-positive signal.
An unexplained benign appearance is not evidence that a high-value payment is safe to release.
An override without evidence turns uncertainty into an unreviewable side effect.
Required control: Keep the invoice quarantined, show the reviewer the flagged span and uncertainty, and preserve the accountable review path.
Required control: Run approved benign and hostile fixtures, then recalibrate or route the screen for review before any payment action.

feedback.reason: Keep the invoice quarantined, show the reviewer the flagged span and uncertainty, run the approved false-positive/benign fixture checks, and recalibrate or route the screen for review before any payment action. The decisive constraint is A false-positive safety signal must not be silently bypassed or treated as proof of an attack; the high-value side effect needs a visible hold, calibrated evidence, and an accountable review path.

options.text: Keep the invoice quarantined, show the reviewer the flagged span and uncertainty, and preserve the accountable review path.
Lower the screen threshold globally so the benign OCR format is less likely to be held.
Ignore the flag because the invoice appears benign and the reviewer is already expecting the payment.
Run approved benign and hostile fixtures, then recalibrate or route the screen for review before any payment action.
Ask the reviewer to override the flag without showing evidence because the payment parameters are already prepared.

questions.prompt: A high-value invoice is correctly isolated as untrusted content, but the input screen flags a new benign OCR format as a possible injection and provides no confidence or evidence for the flag. The payment tool is available and the accountable reviewer is waiting. Select TWO: Which actions handle the unexplained safety flag?

constraints: The email contains an indirect instruction.
The supplier list is unnecessary to draft the order.
Submission is a consequential write action.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the content were trusted internal policy and the assistant had no sensitive-data or write access, tool-result isolation and a submission approval gate would carry less operational value.
details.errorCorrection: System instructions promote attacker text, broad supplier or payment access expands blast radius, plain-text conversion does not remove the instruction threat, and a warning or later review cannot replace least privilege and pre-write approval.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends isolating third-party content in tool_result blocks, screening tool outputs, and limiting sensitive data and actions with least privilege; supplier-list minimization and approval are the scenario's control requirements.
details.scenarioApplication: Pass the email as identified untrusted data, screen the proposed fields, provide no supplier-list data or lookup authority, expose only drafting tools, and require accountable confirmation before submission.
details.transfer: Treat external content as data, minimize both data and tool authority to the task, and enforce human confirmation at consequential side effects.

messages.text: Treating vendor text as ordinary instructions and retaining supplier access lets untrusted content influence a broader surface; a submission warning does not replace draft-only tools and exact approval.
Screening the draft comes after granting unnecessary supplier and payment access, and confirmation alone does not constrain what untrusted content can influence before submission.
Plain-text conversion does not neutralize the untrusted instruction, supplier-list access violates minimization, and post-draft review does not screen the input before it shapes the draft.

feedback.reason: The design isolates attacker-controlled content, removes unnecessary supplier-list access, limits the assistant to drafting, and places an enforceable approval boundary before the write.

options.text: Treat the email as ordinary instructions, expose supplier lookup for matching, and gate only the final submission with a warning.
Keep the email in an identified untrusted tool_result, screen its fields, omit supplier-list data and access, allow draft-only tools, and require approval before submission.
Screen the drafted order after allowing supplier and payment lookups, then require a confirmation before submission.
Convert the email to plain text, retain supplier-list access for matching, gate submission, and review the proposed purchase after the draft is complete.

questions.prompt: A procurement assistant reads an untrusted vendor email, drafts purchase orders, and must not disclose a supplier list or submit a purchase without approval. Which guardrail design is appropriate?

constraints: Only task-relevant context is needed.
Outputs can be filtered and representative interactions audited.
Quality degradation from controls can be measured.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If no proprietary context entered the model and outputs contained only public facts, leak filtering would not be needed for this path.
details.errorCorrection: More exposed context enlarges the surface, prompt disclosure is not a safe boundary, and model size is not an output control.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends separating context, removing unnecessary proprietary details, filtering outputs, and auditing regularly while testing for performance degradation.
details.scenarioApplication: Keep only negotiation facts needed for the task, separate hidden instructions from user content, filter sensitive terms, and review sampled interactions.
details.transfer: Minimize sensitive context and combine output filtering with ongoing leakage and utility checks.

messages.text: More context increases the amount that can be disclosed, and refusals alone are not enforcement.
Prompt disclosure exposes the negotiation terms rather than protecting them.
Capability does not remove the data exposure or provide a deterministic output boundary.

feedback.reason: Reducing exposed data lowers the leak surface, output controls catch disclosure, and audits show whether the controls damage legitimate task quality.

options.text: Add proprietary detail to preserve context, instruct refusal, and rely on model behavior when hidden instructions are requested.
Minimize proprietary context, separate instructions, filter outputs, and audit leakage and task quality.
Expose the full prompt to users, then let them decide which negotiation terms are sensitive.
Increase model size, retain the full prompt, and review leaked terms after deployment.

questions.prompt: A contract assistant has no write tools but can reveal proprietary negotiation terms from a long system prompt when users ask for hidden instructions. What should reduce the leak risk?

constraints: The task needs no production credentials or open network.
Sandboxing, least privilege, and deployment-shaped injection tests are feasible.
Residual risk and stopping conditions can be recorded.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If a package mirror were required and no secrets were needed, an allowlisted egress exception could be tested and documented.
details.errorCorrection: Open egress, benchmarks, and credentials increase blast radius or measure the wrong layer; they do not establish a safe environment.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends process, filesystem, and egress boundaries and notes that credentials absent from the sandbox cannot be exfiltrated through the agent.
details.scenarioApplication: Run the agent with an isolated filesystem and allowlisted network, omit production secrets, exercise hostile inputs, and record the access decision and stop rules.
details.transfer: Contain execution and data paths first, then use realistic hostile tests and an explicit residual-risk decision before expanding authority.

messages.text: Unrestricted egress expands the impact of model or content failure without being required.
Coding quality does not bound secret access, filesystem mutation, or network side effects.
Adding production credentials turns a build helper into a high-impact exfiltration path.
Filesystem and egress containment reduce blast radius and unnecessary authority.
Realistic tests and residual-risk ownership provide evidence for a bounded access decision.

feedback.reason: Containment reduces possible impact, while deployment-shaped tests and explicit residual-risk records show whether the remaining boundary is acceptable.

options.text: Sandbox filesystem and egress and omit credentials and tools the build task does not need.
Grant unrestricted egress because it makes dependency failures easier to debug.
Rely on strong coding benchmarks as evidence that the environment is safe.
Put production credentials in the sandbox so the agent can repair any failed build.
Test hostile content in the actual harness and document residual risk, owners, and stopping conditions before expanding access.

questions.prompt: An autonomous code agent in a shared build environment could read secrets, use unrestricted egress, or alter outputs even though coding tests are strong. Select TWO controls.

constraints: The attack enters through third-party email content.
Forwarding and unrelated-read permissions are unnecessary for the task.
The direct-prompt suite omitted the deployed content and tool surface.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If no email write or unrelated-read tools existed, the same message could affect wording but could not forward other messages.
details.errorCorrection: Direct tests, a caution sentence, or user reports do not exercise the actual indirect path or prevent the side effect.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic describes prompt injections hidden in emails and other content and says defenses must account for tools, data, permissions, and environment choices.
details.scenarioApplication: Replay hostile email fixtures, represent them as untrusted content, restrict reads to the needed mailbox scope, remove forwarding, and inspect outbound destinations.
details.transfer: Threat-test the real content and permission surface, not only direct prompts, and reduce authority to the task minimum.

messages.text: Direct-prompt results omit the email injection path and do not explain forwarding authority.
A sentence is not application enforcement while the forwarding tool remains available.
User reports are late and do not replace adversarial coverage of the deployed path.

feedback.reason: The incident is an indirect injection through email combined with excessive data and action permissions; the deployed surface must be tested and narrowed.

options.text: Treat direct jailbreak coverage as sufficient, classify forwarding as a model issue, and keep current mailbox permissions for continuity.
Replay hostile email fixtures, keep email untrusted, remove unrelated reads and forwarding, and verify egress.
Add an ignore-email sentence, retain forwarding for workflow completeness, and monitor the next batch of outgoing messages.
Disable direct tests, wait for user reports, and review forwarded messages after they reach recipients.

questions.prompt: An inbox agent passes direct jailbreak tests but follows a malicious email instruction to forward unrelated messages because it has forwarding and broad read access. What explains the incident?

constraints: Each failure can be linked to assets, permissions, likelihood evidence, and blast radius.
An accountable owner can accept, mitigate, transfer, or block residual risk.
High-impact unaccepted paths should stop deployment.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If every failure were read-only, reversible, and equally low impact, a simpler inventory could be adequate without separate go/no-go thresholds.
details.errorCorrection: A flat list, frequency-only ranking, or control inventory does not reveal high-impact paths or who can accept their residual risk.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic frames risk across model behavior, external attackers, and the environment or content an agent can reach, then uses hard boundaries to cap blast radius; ranking and acceptance are scenario governance.
details.scenarioApplication: For each risk, record affected asset, reachable authority, evidence, control, residual impact, owner, and the threshold that blocks or permits launch.
details.transfer: Make risk disposition explicit: prioritize impact and reachability, assign an owner, and block unaccepted high-consequence paths.

messages.text: Average quality cannot show which reachable failure has unacceptable impact or who owns it.
Frequency alone can under-rank rare credential exposure or destructive misuse.
A control may reduce but not eliminate risk; residual impact still needs a decision.

feedback.reason: Deployment decisions need consequence and reachability prioritization plus an explicit disposition and owner for what remains after controls.

options.text: Rank risks by impact and reachability, record residual risk, assign owners, and set go/no-go thresholds.
Keep one flat list and approve when average model quality clears target, with owners assigned after deployment.
Prioritize the most frequent error, defer credential exposure, and revisit rare paths during quarterly review.
