feedback.reason: The differing results follow user credential expiry, while the shared endpoint and policy are stable. Repair the identity lifecycle at user scope rather than changing shared configuration.

options.text: Publish the currently working pilot credential through the organization’s secret manager so every developer reconnects under one stable identity.
Move the reviewed endpoint into managed configuration and restart all sessions so the central endpoint becomes authoritative over cached authentication.
Regenerate the project server definition and repeat project approval, preserving the existing user credential records for the new definition.
Verify policy and approval, reconnect affected users through the authorized credential flow, revoke their expired credentials, and check /mcp.

questions.prompt: After the organization’s 30-day credential rotation, some developers can still use the project’s GitHub MCP server while others receive expired-credential errors. The reviewed endpoint and managed allowlist are unchanged. What is the appropriate provisioning repair?

constraints: The team needs a reviewable shared default.
No enforcement mandate or protected-file control is required.
Machine-specific values may vary by contributor.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Project scope is appropriate for a reviewed shared default; a requirement to enforce protected files, network, MCP, or hooks against local changes would justify the managed scope.
details.errorCorrection: User-only copies and local-only files do not provide one reviewed repository contract, while managed settings add authority and an organization-wide owner the requirement does not need.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic documents distinct managed, user, project, and local settings scopes; project settings can be shared with a repository while local and user settings are kept out of version control. The choice of project scope here is the team's scenario policy.
details.scenarioApplication: Commit the reviewed formatter and repository instructions in project settings, document their supported behavior, and leave machine-specific values in local settings.
details.transfer: When a team needs a shareable default without enforcement, put the reviewed contract in project scope and reserve managed scope for an actual organization-wide control.

messages.text: Manual user copies create drift and do not make the repository the shared source of the formatter or instructions.
Managed settings impose organization-wide enforcement beyond the stated distribution need and add an unnecessary control owner.
Local files can vary and cannot provide the reviewed, version-controlled project default the team needs.

feedback.reason: The team needs one reviewed, shareable project default, while the absence of an enforcement mandate does not justify organization-wide managed control.

options.text: Place the formatter in user settings and copy the repository instructions manually, letting each contributor maintain their own version.
Commit the reviewed formatter and instructions in project scope, document the supported behavior, and keep machine-specific values in local scope.
Deploy managed settings across the organization so the defaults cannot be changed, even though no enforcement or protected-file requirement exists.
Keep the formatter and instructions in local scope, compare outputs during team reviews, and avoid a version-controlled project contract.

questions.prompt: A small team wants to share a reviewed formatter and repository instruction set. No organization-wide enforcement or protected-file requirement exists, and the repository is the only shared source the team maintains. Which configuration scope is appropriate?

constraints: The private helper is specific to this repository.
The preference should follow the developer across repositories.
The reviewed default is intended for version control and all contributors.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the helper were intentionally user-wide and not repository-specific, user scope could hold it; if every value were shared and portable, project scope could hold the set.
details.errorCorrection: Putting private or repository-specific values in project scope exposes them to other contributors, while placing the shared default in user or repeated local files loses the repository contract and cross-repository portability.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic documents distinct managed, user, project, and local settings scopes; project settings can be shared with a repository while local and user settings are kept out of version control. The scenario supplies the ownership and disclosure policy for the split.
details.scenarioApplication: Keep the private helper in repository-local settings, the portable preference in user settings, and only the reviewed shared default in project settings; inspect the resolved combination without copying private material.
details.transfer: Assign configuration by both owner and portability: local for repository-private values, user for developer-wide preferences, and project for reviewed team defaults.

messages.text: Project scope would expose a repository-private helper, and a user override does not repair the ownership mistake.
User scope would distribute the personal settings but leave the reviewed project default dependent on each user and repository.
Repeated local copies do not follow the user across repositories and storing the helper beside the project default crosses its disclosure boundary.
Without local/user separation, the repository-private helper can leak or the preference becomes tied to one repository instead of the developer.
Without project scope for the reviewed default and a resolved-state check, contributors lack one shared contract and private values can be copied accidentally.

feedback.reason: The three values have different owners: local scope protects repository-specific private behavior, user scope carries a developer-wide preference, and project scope distributes the reviewed team default.

options.text: Keep the repository-private helper in local settings and the cross-repository preference in user settings; do not commit private values.
Commit the reviewed team default in project settings and verify the effective combination without copying private values into the repository.
Commit the helper and default together in project scope, then let user overrides handle the cross-repository preference.
Put all three values in user settings so personal ownership controls every repository.
Copy the user preference into each repository local file and store the private helper beside the project default.

questions.prompt: A developer needs a repository-local private endpoint/helper that must not be shared with other repositories, a user-wide tool preference, and a reviewed project default that every contributor should receive. Select TWO scope assignments that preserve ownership and portability.

constraints: The preference key is absent from the project file, whose hash matches the other workstations.
The divergence occurs for one engineer only, and the path is machine-local.
User and local settings can be compared without disclosing private values.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the project explicitly set the preference key, the user value would not override it; inspect the local path source instead, and use managed precedence only when a managed source exists.
details.errorCorrection: A user setting does not override a project value when that key is set; adding a shared value or committing the machine path masks the scope evidence, and a fleet reinstall does not identify the owner.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic documents precedence across managed, project, local, and user settings and recommends checking active sources when a value appears ignored. The one-user diagnosis and correction order are supplied by the scenario evidence.
details.scenarioApplication: Confirm that the preference key is absent before using or correcting the user's default, inspect the local path value separately, and verify both resolved results again.
details.transfer: When one workstation diverges, first determine whether a project key is unset and then inspect local machine values before editing a shared contract.

messages.text: The project source already matches the fleet, so replacing it would erase evidence and impose the outlier on everyone.
A project value changes the shared contract and committing a machine path creates portability drift; neither action identifies the unset-key default or local owner.
A fleet reinstall treats a scoped configuration difference as a tool defect before the active settings sources have been compared.

feedback.reason: A user default applies when the project key is unset, while a machine-local value explains the path difference; scope comparison can correct each owner without changing the shared contract.

options.text: Replace the unchanged project file with the outlier preference and path, then ask all engineers to pull and compare behavior.
Add a project value to force the preference, and store the machine path in the shared file so every checkout resolves alike.
Check whether the project key is unset, inspect the local path source, correct the owning value, and recheck the resolved settings.
Reinstall the shared tool on every workstation before comparing scopes, treating the one-user divergence as a fleet defect.

questions.prompt: The same repository settings work for nine engineers, but one engineer sees a different tool preference for a key absent from the project file and a different local path after an upgrade. No managed policy applies, and the project file is unchanged. What should the team diagnose first?

constraints: The supported release range is declared.
A representative older installation can be tested.
The project file is the intended shared distribution surface.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the fleet were on one validated release and the key were covered by its settings reference, the project rollout could proceed through the normal review.
details.errorCorrection: An untested ignored key can produce silent fleet divergence, while user or local exceptions turn a shared project contract into an unowned compatibility split.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic documents distinct managed, user, project, and local settings scopes; project settings can be shared with a repository while local and user settings are kept out of version control. Version validation and the minimum-version decision are scenario controls.
details.scenarioApplication: Test the key on every supported release, communicate a validated minimum version or defer the setting, then roll out the versioned project configuration with a compatibility check.
details.transfer: Before making a shared configuration key canonical, validate it across the supported client range and assign ownership for version compatibility.

messages.text: Older installations may resolve the repository differently, and reported differences are not a compatibility check before rollout.
Per-user enablement hides the shared default and makes behavior dependent on manual reconciliation instead of the reviewed project file.
Ad hoc local exceptions leave no explicit supported-version contract and can produce inconsistent behavior across the fleet.

feedback.reason: A shared project setting is portable only after compatibility is established across the declared supported range; otherwise the team must make the version boundary explicit or defer the key.

options.text: Commit the key across the fleet, document the newer release, and let older installations ignore it while contributors report behavior differences.
Validate the key across supported releases, set or communicate a minimum version or defer it, then roll out the versioned project settings.
Leave the project file unchanged, enable the key in each user setting, and reconcile behavior manually when contributors report differences.
Keep the key project-wide for newer installations, move it locally for older ones, and omit a supported-version policy or compatibility check.

questions.prompt: A team wants to adopt a settings key documented for a newer Claude Code release while supporting a mixed fleet. The project file is shared, but the oldest supported release has not been validated against that key. What rollout decision fits?

constraints: The project file must remain a portable shared contract.
The editor and hook paths are machine-specific.
Clean checkouts can be tested on every supported operating system.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the paths were portable on every supported OS, they could remain project-scoped after the same clean-checkout verification.
details.errorCorrection: Keeping machine paths committed creates recurring checkout edits and drift, while moving the whole file or relying on informal overrides loses a canonical shared contract.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic documents distinct managed, user, project, and local settings scopes; project settings can be shared with a repository while local and user settings are kept out of version control. Portability classification and the verification plan are scenario policy.
details.scenarioApplication: Retain portable shared keys in the project file, move editor and machine hook paths to local settings, and verify the resolved result from clean checkouts on each supported OS.
details.transfer: Keep shared configuration portable in project scope, isolate machine-specific values locally, and verify the resolved configuration on each supported environment.

messages.text: Committed machine paths force local edits and leave the shared file nonportable across the supported operating systems.
Moving portable shared keys to user scope removes the repository contract and makes reproducibility depend on personal configuration.
An informal primary-OS path and overrides still create unmanaged divergence and do not establish a portable project value.
Without the project/local split, the repository still encodes machine-specific values and clean checkouts can continue to fail.
Without cross-OS clean-checkout evidence, the team cannot show that the repaired scopes resolve the intended portable contract.

feedback.reason: The project contract can be reproducible only when it contains portable shared values; machine-specific paths belong in local scope and the repaired combination needs cross-OS verification.

options.text: Keep portable workflow keys in project scope, and move the OS-specific editor and machine hook paths to local scope.
Test clean checkouts on every supported OS and record the resolved settings for the repaired project/local split.
Keep machine paths in project scope and ask each contributor to edit the checkout after pulling the shared file.
Move the entire file to user scope so each contributor can repair paths without changing the repository contract.
Commit one project path for the primary OS and let other OS users override it informally.

questions.prompt: A team commits a project settings file for a reproducible workflow, but it contains an OS-specific editor path and machine-specific hook path that break a clean checkout on the other supported operating systems. Select TWO scope repairs that restore portability.

constraints: The restrictions must survive edits to user and project configuration.
Administrators control the organization-managed configuration source.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the rules were optional team defaults, versioned project settings or a plugin could be sufficient and easier for developers to adapt.
details.errorCorrection: Repository review, provisioned defaults, and shared plugins can distribute conventions, but each still needs the stated non-editable enforcement boundary.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic says managed settings can lock down tools, sandbox execution, MCP servers, and hooks, with policy taking precedence over local configuration.
details.scenarioApplication: Administrators configure the managed tool, network, MCP, and hook restrictions, then inspect resolved sessions to confirm that the intended source is active.
details.transfer: Choose a configuration scope according to who must be able to override it, then verify the effective policy rather than just the distributed file.

messages.text: Code-owner review governs committed changes, but a developer can change a local checkout before that review; the scenario requires stronger enforcement.
Periodic reconciliation can detect drift after it occurs, but an editable user setting does not outrank local choices continuously.
A plugin packages behavior for reuse. Installing its approved version does not by itself make its controls an organization-managed policy.

feedback.reason: The required property is enforcement above developer-editable scopes. Managed policy provides that boundary; distribution and review alone do not make a local setting authoritative.

options.text: Commit shared permission rules, MCP definitions, and hooks in each repository; require code-owner review before changing those files.
Distribute a standard user settings file through workstation provisioning, and periodically compare developer copies with the approved version.
Put the enforced controls in managed settings and verify the effective policy in representative sessions.
Install a shared team plugin containing the restrictions and validate its version when a developer opens a repository.

questions.prompt: An engineering organization must restrict Claude Code to approved MCP servers and network destinations, and preserve protected-file hooks across every project. Developers need freedom to edit ordinary repository settings. Which configuration approach meets the enforcement requirement?

constraints: The server’s requested scopes and fetched content can be reviewed.
The organization requires an allowlist, project approval, workspace trust, and individual credentials.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A contained pilot can use a narrower provisioning process, but its successful connection is not sufficient evidence for organization-wide rollout.
details.errorCorrection: Pilot connectivity, transport security, and read-only capability address different properties; none replaces review of external content and the required trust decisions.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic tells users to verify trust before connecting MCP servers because servers that fetch external content can expose prompt-injection risk.
details.scenarioApplication: Review the server and permissions, distribute only nonsecret project configuration, verify the required allowlist and approvals, and let each developer authenticate and inspect /mcp status.
details.transfer: When moving an integration from one user to a team, recheck the trust and authority boundaries rather than copying a working connection.

messages.text: Replication and connectivity checks can reproduce a working setup while leaving project review and each contributor’s approval state unresolved.
Provider identity and transport security do not establish that fetched user-controlled text is trustworthy or that requested scopes are appropriate.
Read-only tools can still expose untrusted content and sensitive data; reduced write authority does not confer project trust.

feedback.reason: Connectivity proves that a connection works, not that the rollout satisfies trust, scope, and identity requirements. External issue text remains an untrusted input even through a familiar provider.

options.text: Replicate the pilot’s user-level configuration on every workstation, then use successful connectivity checks as the rollout acceptance test.
Review scopes and external-content exposure, publish nonsecret project configuration, verify required trust and approvals, and test each user’s connection.
Approve the integration from the provider’s identity and encrypted transport, then focus rollout checks on consistent tool names and schema versions.
Limit the server to read operations and record its endpoint centrally; use that reduced capability as the basis for automatic project trust.

questions.prompt: A team is rolling out a reviewed GitHub MCP integration that fetches issue text written by external users. A pilot account connects successfully. Which rollout procedure best addresses the remaining team-level risk?

constraints: Reviewed invoice fixtures and integration checks exist.
A reviewer can inspect the diff and billing criteria in a fresh context.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: These checks require time, but are proportionate to financial output correctness. They complement rather than replace focused unit tests.
details.errorCorrection: More tests derived from the new code, a single illustrative invoice, and coverage percentages can repeat the same assumptions without establishing billing correctness.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends a fresh-context review of the diff and explicit criteria before counting unattended work as done.
details.scenarioApplication: Run the external contract checks, then ask a separate review context to assess the diff against billing requirements. Correct or explicitly disposition findings before accepting the change.
details.transfer: Combine independently grounded executable evidence with review that does not inherit the implementation’s reasoning.

messages.text: Tests derived from the same explanation may reinforce the original mistaken assumption; confidence comparison is not an independent contract check.
A fresh context helps independence, but one illustrative invoice does not exercise the available reviewed billing cases or a systematic diff review.
Branch coverage shows which paths executed, not whether their arithmetic matches the independently specified invoice contract.
Reviewed fixtures and integration cases provide executable expectations that do not originate in the refactor’s new assumptions.
A fresh review of the diff against explicit criteria can expose missing cases that the implementation and its tests share.

feedback.reason: Pre-existing reviewed fixtures challenge the billing contract independently of the new implementation, while a fresh review can identify omitted cases and shared assumptions.

options.text: Run the reviewed invoice fixtures and integration checks against the changed module and inspect any mismatches.
Have the implementation session create additional tests from its explanation of the refactor, then compare its before-and-after confidence.
Compare output totals for one representative invoice in a fresh session and accept the change if the explanation matches the implementation notes.
Give a fresh reviewer the diff and billing criteria, investigate the reported gaps, and record their disposition.
Increase coverage of the new helper functions using cases derived from their current branches, and use the coverage gain as the acceptance criterion.

questions.prompt: Claude Code has refactored a billing module in an isolated branch. Its new unit tests pass, but they were written from the same assumptions as the implementation and may miss changes to invoice totals. Select TWO checks that provide meaningfully independent evidence before merge.

constraints: The observed regression follows context accumulation, with no identified repository or model change.
The active acceptance criteria and focused tests are available.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Clearing requires a deliberate handoff of current state. If the conversation is already short and relevant, investigate the actual failing implementation instead.
details.errorCorrection: Repeating instructions, changing models, or adding a reviewer may help other problems, but leaves the identified context pollution in the implementation session.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic says context fills quickly and performance can degrade, recommending /clear between tasks and /compact for controlled summaries.
details.scenarioApplication: Checkpoint the partial change. Compact around the active API task, or clear when changing tasks, then supply the needed constraints and run focused tests and diff review.
details.transfer: When performance deteriorates with accumulated context, preserve state and reduce the working set before adding more instructions or tools.

messages.text: Repeated reminders add to the overloaded history and do not remove irrelevant material competing with the active constraint.
A model change is not evidence that the noisy context has become appropriate; the identified cause should be addressed directly.
Independent review can detect errors, but the implementation agent remains exposed to the same context problem while producing further changes.

feedback.reason: The immediate problem is an overloaded working context. Preserve the useful work, remove irrelevant history, and restore the current objective and verification loop before continuing.

options.text: Restate the API constraint at the end of each message and retain the complete history so earlier implementation evidence remains directly visible.
Switch to a more capable model in the same session and use the next focused test result to determine whether additional context repair is necessary.
Checkpoint, reduce context with a focused /compact or /clear at a task boundary, restore the active criteria, and verify the next diff.
Ask a second agent to inspect the current diff while the implementation agent continues in its existing session, then apply the reviewer’s findings.

questions.prompt: During a long Claude Code session, completed tasks, repeated build logs, and unrelated file dumps have accumulated. The agent now misses a previously stated API constraint. The active change is still useful and can be checkpointed. What should the developer do first?

constraints: The manifest identifies idempotent transformations and completed checkpoints.
Partial module changes can be inspected and isolated.
A failed module must remain visible for review.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the entire transformation were verified idempotent and a whole-run replay were cheaper than reconciliation, replay could be reasonable. That assurance is not given for the partial state here.
details.errorCorrection: Whole-tree replay may repeat side effects, file modification does not prove completion, and conversation continuity does not replace a durable execution record.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic describes durable execution with resumable state and deterministic safeguards such as retry logic and regular checkpoints for long-running agents.
details.scenarioApplication: Match completed entries to recorded diffs and checks, inspect or isolate the unfinished module, and resume the remaining idempotent units. Record failures rather than counting partial work as success.
details.transfer: After interruption, reconcile durable completion evidence with actual state before choosing what to repeat.

messages.text: Final tests may not detect repeated side effects or unnecessary modifications; the available checkpoint evidence permits a more precise recovery.
An unverified partial edit can look modified without satisfying the module contract, so this would skip unfinished work.
The manifest contains recorded execution evidence that a reconstructed conversation or file-layout inference may miss.

feedback.reason: Recovery must use authoritative checkpoint and working-tree evidence. A changed file is not proof of a completed transformation, and replay is safe only where its behavior is known.

options.text: Reconcile the manifest with the working diff, preserve verified modules, inspect the partial module, and resume pending checkpoints with their checks.
Restart the migration over the working tree and rely on the final repository tests to detect whether repeated transformations changed completed modules.
Mark every module with a modified file as completed, then run the migration only on unchanged files and perform one final integration check.
Restore the last conversational summary and let the agent infer the next module from the current file layout, using the manifest only if a test fails.

questions.prompt: A network interruption stops a multi-hour migration halfway through a repository. A durable manifest records completed modules, their diff identities and passing checks; another module has an unverified partial diff. What is the safest continuation?

constraints: The owner can clarify authorization and acceptance.
The assistant can inspect and plan interactively.
The later verification checks are known.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Once the contract, file set, and checks are explicit and repeatable, a bounded noninteractive run can be appropriate for later iterations.
details.errorCorrection: A passing test may omit the owner-defined authorization boundary, and restricted or headless execution cannot resolve ambiguous intent in a sensitive flow.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends separating research and planning from implementation and using explicit verification checks after code changes. The requirement to clarify authorization before automation is scenario policy.
details.scenarioApplication: Inspect and plan interactively with the owner, record the approved authorization and checks, implement after clarification, and reserve claude -p for a later bounded repeatable run if one exists.
details.transfer: Use interactive exploration and owner clarification while authorization is unresolved; move to headless execution only after the repository contract is explicit and repeatable.

messages.text: Restricted tools limit possible actions but do not establish what the owner authorizes or which authentication behavior the patch must preserve.
Tests may pass without encoding the missing owner decision, so implementation before clarification makes the wrong contract harder to detect.
A narrow batch still automates an unresolved security boundary; tool restriction is not a substitute for the required human checkpoint.

feedback.reason: The missing authentication contract is an intent and authority question, so the owner checkpoint must precede automation; restricted tools reduce authority but do not supply the missing decision.

options.text: Run claude -p with restricted tools, infer the authentication boundary from existing files, and let tests reveal whether the interpretation was acceptable.
Clarify authorization interactively with the owner, record the approved plan and checks, implement afterward, and reserve claude -p for a later repeatable run.
Start an interactive implementation without owner questions, then use the passing test suite as the authority for the missing authentication contract.
Create a headless batch with a narrow file list, defer the owner decision, and treat restricted tools as sufficient control for the sensitive flow.

questions.prompt: A one-off change in an unfamiliar repository has an unresolved authentication contract and a repository owner is available to answer questions. The change will touch a security-sensitive flow, and no bounded headless batch is needed. Which execution mode should come first?

constraints: The failed fixture and explicit scope-violation finding are independent evidence.
The trusted pre-change checkpoint can be restored.
No dependent work has been built on the unaccepted patch.
Team recovery policy requires restoring the trusted checkpoint after an independent scope violation.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the diff stayed within authorized scope and only the invoice fixture failed, a bounded in-place repair with independent rerun could be appropriate; a scope violation changes the recovery boundary.
details.errorCorrection: An in-place bounded fix can be valid after a functional failure when scope remains authorized; here the independent scope violation makes continuing from the diff unsafe, and a smoke run cannot replace the contract check.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends a fresh-context review of the diff and explicit criteria before counting unattended work as done. The scenario requires checkpoint restoration because the independent review found an unauthorized scope change.
details.scenarioApplication: Restore or quarantine the failed diff to the trusted checkpoint, preserve the failed fixture and scope finding, revise the plan against them, and rerun independent checks before another patch.
details.transfer: Distinguish a repairable in-scope functional failure from an unauthorized diff: restore a trusted checkpoint for the latter, and preserve independent evidence in both cases.

messages.text: A bounded in-place fix could be appropriate for an in-scope fixture failure, but the explicit unauthorized scope change makes this diff an untrusted repair base.
A waiver leaves the failed invoice contract unresolved and builds dependent work on a state the independent review did not accept.
A smoke suite may add evidence but cannot turn the failed independent fixture into a passing contract or establish the correct scope.

feedback.reason: The independent scope violation makes the current diff an untrusted continuation point; restoring or quarantining it preserves a trusted baseline, while a failed test alone could support a bounded in-place repair.

options.text: Apply a bounded invoice-only fix in the existing diff and rerun that fixture, since no other behavior changed.
Restore the trusted checkpoint or quarantine the failed diff, preserve evidence, revise the plan, and rerun independent checks before applying another patch.
Keep the patch in place, add a waiver for the invoice fixture, and let owner acceptance follow after dependent work is built.
Retain the diff, rerun a broader smoke suite, and use the resulting green run as the next baseline without resolving the contract failure.

questions.prompt: An AI-assisted patch was applied from a trusted clean checkpoint, but an independent contract test fails on an invoice total and a fresh review confirms that the diff includes an unauthorized file or scope change. The team can restore the trusted checkpoint and retain the failed evidence. What is the next action?

constraints: The changes are independent.
Separate branches are available.
Each result must be tested before merge.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If one change depended on the other, coordinate a sequence or shared handoff instead of treating the work as independent parallel edits; keep any shared service or secret isolation as a separate environment control.
details.errorCorrection: A shared checkout or worktree lets nearby edits and repository test state mix before attribution is established; commit tags alone do not provide separate working directories, and worktrees do not isolate external dependencies.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic documents worktrees as separate working directories and branches for parallel sessions, and says a fresh worktree may require its own dependency and environment setup. Worktrees do not automatically isolate shared services, ports, or secrets; separate review and merge are scenario controls.
details.scenarioApplication: Create a worktree and branch for each independent change, provision its documented environment, run its tests there, and merge only results that have been reviewed.
details.transfer: Use separate worktrees for independent parallel changes, provision each environment, and merge only independently tested and reviewed results.

messages.text: Alternating branches in one checkout still shares checkout files and repository state, so the two test results are not attributable to separate starting states.
A combined diff loses ownership and can hide which change caused a failed test before either result is reviewed.
Commit tags provide history but do not isolate working files or repository setup state while both engineers edit.

feedback.reason: Independent simultaneous edits need separate working directories and branches so checkout files and branch history from one change cannot silently become the other's starting state; external services remain a separate environment concern.

options.text: Use one checkout, alternate branches, and run each test after the other engineer commits before starting the next edit.
Create a worktree and branch per change, set up each environment, run isolated checks, and merge only reviewed results.
Let both engineers edit the shared checkout, then compare the combined diff and test output before choosing a branch.
Share one worktree but tag each commit, assuming nearby files make isolation unnecessary.

questions.prompt: Two engineers need to make independent changes to the same repository at the same time. Their edits touch nearby files, and each change needs its own tests before the results are merged. Which setup fits?

constraints: The worktree setup instructions and dependency manifests are available.
The failure occurs before patch evaluation.
The main checkout can remain a comparison.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If setup were verified and the same test failed after patch execution, investigate the patch against its independent contract instead of repeating environment provisioning.
details.errorCorrection: Changing the model or prompt confuses an environment failure with patch behavior, while copying unreviewed state or testing only in main hides the worktree contract.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic documents worktrees as separate working directories and branches for parallel sessions, and says a fresh worktree may require its own dependency and environment setup. The order of setup and patch evaluation is scenario policy.
details.scenarioApplication: Provision the documented dependencies and environment in the worktree, verify the checkout-specific setup, rerun the same tests, and keep main as a comparison.
details.transfer: Diagnose a fresh-worktree failure as an environment-readiness issue until its dependencies and settings are provisioned and verified.

messages.text: The worktree has not reached patch evaluation, so changing generation variables does not test the actual failure cause.
Unreviewed environment copying can import hidden state and make the new checkout appear valid without proving its documented setup.
Testing only in main cannot establish that the requested branch and its own worktree environment are runnable.

feedback.reason: The command failed before the patch was evaluated, and a fresh worktree has its own setup requirements; repair and verify that environment before attributing the result to the patch or generation variables.

options.text: Change the prompt or model after the worktree command fails, treating the main checkout’s passing tests as evidence against the patch.
Provision the documented worktree dependencies and environment, verify setup, rerun the same tests, and retain main as a comparison.
Copy main’s untracked environment files into the worktree without review, then accept the patch if the command completes.
Abandon the worktree and test only in main, where the dependency directory and environment are already present.

questions.prompt: A fresh worktree checks out the requested branch, but its dependency directory and local environment are absent; the same tests pass in the main checkout. The patch itself has not been evaluated yet. What should happen first?

constraints: The declared scope and independent checks are recorded.
Fresh review found no unmet criterion.
The owner acceptance and next merge or rollout step are documented.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If a criterion, independent fixture, scope check, or owner acceptance were missing, block the phase and obtain the missing evidence before accepting.
details.errorCorrection: Open-ended review has no defined stopping condition once the declared criteria pass, while merging without the recorded owner decision loses the lifecycle evidence that supports acceptance.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends a fresh-context review of the diff and explicit criteria before counting unattended work as done. The acceptance and stop decision follows the scenario’s complete evidence and owner checkpoint.
details.scenarioApplication: Accept the scoped patch, record the evidence and owner decision, and move to the agreed merge or rollout; reopen only when new evidence or a scope change creates a new decision.
details.transfer: Stop at a defined acceptance boundary when independent evidence and ownership converge; reopen only for a changed risk, requirement, or scope.

messages.text: Additional review without a new risk or unmet criterion replaces the defined acceptance boundary with an unbounded search.
Expanding scope introduces a new change to review and defeats the declared narrow patch instead of closing its acceptance decision.
Passing fixtures do not replace the required recorded owner acceptance and lifecycle evidence.

feedback.reason: The declared scope, independent checks, fresh review, and owner acceptance converge on the acceptance boundary; more review without a new risk or changed requirement adds delay rather than evidence.

options.text: Accept the scoped patch, record evidence and owner decision, and proceed to the agreed merge or rollout; reopen if scope or evidence changes.
Request additional model reviews and broader tests until every hypothetical risk has been discussed, despite all declared criteria passing.
Expand the patch scope before merge so a larger review can search for risks outside the declared acceptance criteria.
Merge without recording owner acceptance because passing independent fixtures make lifecycle evidence self-authenticating.

questions.prompt: A narrowly scoped patch passes the independent contract fixtures, the diff contains only declared files, a fresh-context review finds no unmet criterion, and the owner has accepted the recorded evidence. What is the lifecycle decision?

constraints: The change touches session creation, middleware, and logout.
The developer can review a plan before implementation.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A small change in a well-understood module may need less planning. The unfamiliar cross-module security flow warrants an explicit exploration step.
details.errorCorrection: Branches, isolated tests, and specification review are useful controls, but do not replace learning the actual integration contract before choosing an implementation.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends separating research and planning from implementation and using explicit verification checks after code changes.
details.scenarioApplication: Inspect the session utilities and relevant tests, identify affected modules and security cases, review the plan, and give Claude executable checks to run after the scoped implementation.
details.transfer: In unfamiliar code, establish repository fit before implementation and define observable checks that can challenge the resulting change.

messages.text: Isolation makes changes reversible, but learning conventions only from failing tests can miss untested session and security contracts.
An isolated module can pass its own tests while introducing a competing session architecture that does not fit existing callers.
Reviewing the feature specification without inspecting the repository leaves its current session contracts unknown until after implementation.

feedback.reason: The missing information is the existing repository contract. Exploration before planning and editing prevents a plausible standard implementation from taking the wrong architectural path.

options.text: Create an isolated branch, implement a standard authentication pattern, and use the existing tests to identify differences from the repository’s conventions.
Inspect the repository’s authentication paths, agree on a scoped plan and security checks, then implement and verify the change.
Build the new authentication module in isolation from the existing session utilities, then integrate once its own contract tests pass.
Ask a fresh reviewer to assess the feature specification, implement that reviewed specification, and compare the resulting diff with the current utilities.

questions.prompt: A developer asks Claude Code to add authentication across several modules in an unfamiliar repository. Existing session utilities and security tests are available, but their contracts have not yet been inspected. Which workflow provides the best starting point?

constraints: No interactive discussion is needed for routine repositories.
Failures must be isolated and assigned for review.
Automation can parse structured command output.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Noninteractive execution needs orchestration and result handling. Ambiguous repositories should leave the routine path and receive focused review.
details.errorCorrection: A shared interactive history mixes state, disposable branches do not bound tool authority, and a model’s success summary is not test evidence.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends claude -p for CI and scripts, structured output for programmatic processing, and restricted tools when running unattended.
details.scenarioApplication: Refine the prompt during the pilot, invoke each repository independently with the permitted tools and structured output, run its checks, and retain explicit failed outcomes for the owner.
details.transfer: Scale a repeatable AI-assisted workflow through constrained independent runs with per-unit evidence, not a single growing conversation.

messages.text: Checkpointed summaries help continuity, but one shared session still couples repository state and does not supply the requested independent structured execution records.
A disposable branch limits Git changes, not all tool effects; a central build can also omit repository-specific migration checks.
A confident final summary can be wrong. Skipping checks for apparently routine runs removes the evidence needed to classify success.

feedback.reason: The repeatable task fits noninteractive execution, but safe scaling depends on bounded tools, separate repository state, machine-readable results, and actual verification for each run.

options.text: Run one long-lived interactive session over repositories in sequence, checkpointing its summary after each repository to preserve migration context.
Launch unrestricted noninteractive runs in disposable branches, then use a central build result as the gate for merging the successful-looking changes.
Invoke a separate noninteractive run per repository and classify success from its final prose summary, with tests reserved for repositories that report uncertainty.
Use constrained claude -p runs per repository, collect structured output, execute each repository’s checks, and route failures for review.

questions.prompt: A platform team has a bounded dependency migration to apply to 60 repositories. The prompt, allowed files, and deterministic checks are defined, and unattended runs need repository-specific success or failure records. How should the team scale after a small pilot?

constraints: Provider request identifiers and classified error responses are available.
A bounded reproduction can run in safe mode.
Detailed diagnostics require controlled handling.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: More detailed diagnostics may be justified for a specific unresolved incident, but should be collected deliberately in a controlled environment rather than by default.
details.errorCorrection: Prompt hashes do not replace provider request IDs; broad project differences confound isolation; routine full diagnostics collect more sensitive content than the runbook permits.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends safe mode to test plugins, MCP servers, and hooks, and warns that detailed diagnostics may contain conversation content or credentials.
details.scenarioApplication: Record the request identifier and error category for each incident, then use a bounded reproduction to compare customization states. Keep any detailed artifacts under the prescribed sensitive-data controls.
details.transfer: Separate the evidence needed for request correlation from the additional data needed for a bounded local reproduction.

messages.text: A content cluster may help grouping, but it cannot identify the exact provider request and can combine different executions of the same prompt.
Comparing a new minimal project with the full project changes more than the suspected customization, making attribution less reliable than a controlled mode comparison.
Restricted storage limits access but does not satisfy the requirement to avoid routine retention of sensitive prompt-bearing diagnostics.
Request IDs and bounded error metadata connect the failure to support evidence without storing prompt text by default.
Safe-mode comparison and selective re-enablement isolate the customization while retaining the managed-policy boundary.

feedback.reason: Request metadata supplies direct correlation without routine prompt storage. A controlled safe-mode comparison isolates customizations without treating organization policy as a debugging variable.

options.text: Cluster failures by a hash of the prompt and use that cluster identifier as the primary reference in provider support requests.
Retain request IDs, error classes, and bounded timing metadata; enable sensitive diagnostics only in a controlled reproduction.
Create a fresh project configuration containing just the suspected server, then infer the effect of that server by comparing it with the full production project.
Export full session diagnostics into the restricted support archive for every failure so later investigations always have a complete reconstruction.
Compare the reproduction in safe mode and normal mode, re-enable the suspected customization selectively, and preserve managed policy.

questions.prompt: A support runbook must correlate Claude API failures with provider investigations without storing sensitive prompt text. It must also isolate a suspected MCP customization while leaving organization policy intact. Select TWO suitable controls.

constraints: Work can be checkpointed before reducing context.
The same bounded workload can be repeated in normal and safe modes.
Detailed diagnostic artifacts may contain conversation content or credentials.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the controlled reproduction remained slow without customizations and with focused context, profiling in a protected environment would be a reasonable next diagnostic step.
details.errorCorrection: More resources can mask the symptom, profiling alone is less targeted than the available configuration contrast, and changing two variables together does not isolate causality.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends compacting, restarting, and using safe mode to isolate customizations, and warns that heap snapshots can contain conversations and credentials.
details.scenarioApplication: Preserve the active work, establish a compact or fresh-session reproduction, compare safe mode with the same workload, and reintroduce plugins, servers, or hooks individually.
details.transfer: When a successful comparison changes several factors, hold the workload steady and reintroduce one factor at a time.

messages.text: A higher limit may reduce resource pressure but does not reveal whether accumulated context or a customization caused the regression.
Protected profiling is legitimate, but the observed safe-mode/fresh-session contrast offers a narrower first isolation test before interpreting a large mixed-state snapshot.
Removing a customization while also compacting context confounds the result; either change could account for the improvement.

feedback.reason: The working comparison changed both context and customizations. A controlled workload with staged context reduction and one-at-a-time re-enablement can distinguish those causes without conflating them.

options.text: Raise the process resource limit and compare completion time on the original session, using the faster result to decide whether customizations need changes.
Checkpoint and reduce context, repeat a fixed workload in safe mode, then re-enable customizations individually; handle detailed diagnostics as sensitive.
Profile the original long-running process first, collect a heap snapshot in restricted storage, and prioritize its largest allocations before testing configuration differences.
Disable the most recently installed customization and compact the session together, then attribute any improvement to that customization and deploy its removal.

questions.prompt: Claude Code consumes unusually high CPU in a large repository. A fresh session with customizations disabled behaves normally, while the affected session contains large build outputs. How should the operator isolate the cause?

constraints: CI environment details, resolved settings, plugin versions, and request IDs can be captured.
Safe mode and reversible plugin rollback are available.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the same noninteractive failure occurred with the known-good plugin and in safe mode, broaden the investigation to other CI differences rather than continuing to blame the plugin.
details.errorCorrection: Interactive success, a model change, and a combined upgrade alter or omit the variables needed to isolate the CI/plugin regression.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends safe mode to test plugins, MCP servers, and hooks, and warns that detailed diagnostics may contain conversation content or credentials.
details.scenarioApplication: Record the CI configuration and request identifiers, reproduce with pinned inputs, compare safe mode, and test the known-good plugin or a bounded bisect. Keep rollback reversible and retain the diagnostic record.
details.transfer: Reproduce a regression in the actual failing execution mode before changing unrelated configuration.

messages.text: The interactive path already succeeds; repeating it does not test the noninteractive plugin behavior that fails in CI.
A model change introduces another variable before the observed plugin and execution-mode difference has been isolated.
Updating both components can make the symptom disappear without identifying its cause and can discard the known-good comparison.

feedback.reason: The failing execution mode and changed customization are central evidence. Reproducing that mode with controlled versions allows attribution; a successful interactive run is not equivalent.

options.text: Reproduce the prompt interactively using the newest plugin, then treat a successful local run as evidence that the CI host needs rebuilding.
Pin the previous model version in CI and rerun the existing job; use any recovery to decide whether the plugin update is compatible.
Install the latest CLI and plugin together in both environments, then compare their final outputs to establish a common supported configuration.
Capture effective CI inputs and versions, reproduce the noninteractive failure, compare safe mode, and bisect or roll back the plugin while preserving evidence.

questions.prompt: After a plugin update, claude -p fails in CI while an interactive local session succeeds on the same repository and prompt. The last known-good plugin version is available. What investigation should precede a model or prompt change?

constraints: The failure occurs before an HTTP response.
DNS, proxy, and TLS evidence is available.
No provider request identifier or response body exists.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If an HTTP response and request ID were present, preserve that ID and classify the documented response before choosing retry or owner routing.
details.errorCorrection: A provider status check or escalation can be recorded later, but bounded HTTP retry and alternate-runner comparison do not replace diagnosis of the captured pre-response transport failure.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic includes a unique request ID in responses and errors so operators can correlate a failing request with their own traces and support investigations. The pre-response transport diagnosis follows the scenario evidence.
details.scenarioApplication: Preserve DNS/proxy/TLS evidence, verify the failing runner and destination configuration, reproduce there, and defer provider request-ID analysis until an HTTP response exists.
details.transfer: Choose the diagnostic layer supported by the evidence: transport before response, provider correlation after a response and request identifier.

messages.text: Status or escalation with a timestamp may support a later incident, but the captured DNS, proxy, and TLS failure must be diagnosed before assigning it to provider execution.
HTTP retry-after semantics apply to a response; with no response received, retrying before transport diagnosis does not establish provider execution or repair the runner path.
A second runner can be useful after preserving the evidence, but comparing provider behavior first changes the experiment before the failing runner's transport path is understood.

feedback.reason: No response was received to correlate, so the evidence is at the runner transport boundary; provider request-ID analysis becomes relevant only after an HTTP response is received.

options.text: Check provider status and escalate with the runner region, destination, and failure timestamp, treating the lack of a response as a provider-side incident.
Preserve transport evidence, verify DNS/proxy/TLS and runner configuration, reproduce there, and correlate a provider ID only after an HTTP response.
Apply a bounded retry using documented HTTP retry-after semantics before examining DNS, proxy, and TLS, since another call may return an identifier.
Run the same job from a second runner and compare provider behavior before inspecting the failing runner’s DNS and proxy configuration.

questions.prompt: A CI job fails before receiving any HTTP response. DNS resolution and TLS/proxy diagnostics are captured, while no provider request identifier or response error body exists. What diagnostic layer comes first?

constraints: Safe mode removes customizations but leaves core execution and managed controls active.
The clean user/project comparison succeeds.
Managed policy and environment state must remain in force.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If both safe mode and clean user/project configuration failed after managed policy and environment checks matched, repository, runtime, or external-service investigation would be justified.
details.errorCorrection: Managed-policy, plugin, or authentication checks can support later escalation, but fixed core controls and clean user/project success first localize the repair to the user/project layer.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic notes that safe mode disables customizations while authentication, model, built-in tools, permissions, and managed hooks/settings remain; comparing a clean configuration isolates user and project settings. Keeping managed controls is scenario policy.
details.scenarioApplication: Compare and correct the implicated user or project setting, preserve managed policy, rerun the bounded task, and escalate externally only if the clean configuration and managed/environment checks also fail.
details.transfer: Use a clean user/project comparison to isolate configuration layers, and keep managed controls fixed while deciding whether external escalation is warranted.

messages.text: Managed policy and environment were unchanged, and the clean user/project result already localizes the repair; rechecking them does not justify provider attribution first.
The clean user/project success already distinguishes the implicated configuration layer; further plugin bisection treats fixed safe-mode evidence as unresolved external evidence.
Authentication and provider access were unchanged during the contrast; another-runner check can follow only if the clean configuration and managed/environment checks also fail.

feedback.reason: Safe mode alone does not prove an external cause: the clean user/project success isolates those configuration layers while authentication, built-ins, permissions, and managed controls remain unchanged.

options.text: Recompare managed policy and environment state, leave them fixed, and decide whether the provider is external before correcting user/project settings.
Bisect remaining plugins one at a time, leave the clean user/project result secondary, and decide on provider escalation if safe mode still fails.
Compare and correct the user/project setting, keep managed controls intact, rerun, and escalate externally only if clean and managed/environment checks also fail.
Recheck authentication configuration and provider access on another runner before correcting the implicated user/project setting.

questions.prompt: A failure remains in safe mode, but a clean user and project configuration makes the same bounded task succeed. Authentication, model, built-in tools, permissions, managed hooks, and managed settings remain unchanged during the comparison. What should be repaired?

constraints: Lower-sensitivity metadata and redacted reproduction were tried first.
Authorization, access, restricted storage, and deletion controls are recorded.
Routine telemetry does not need prompt retention.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Without named authorization, restricted storage, or a deletion rule, remain with redacted metadata and safe-mode reproduction rather than collecting detailed diagnostics.
details.errorCorrection: Normal full capture creates unnecessary exposure, while blanket refusal ignores a proportionate authorized investigation; indefinite retention exceeds the approved purpose and deletion boundary.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends safe mode first and explains that detailed diagnostics or heap snapshots can contain conversation content and credentials, so sensitive captures require careful handling. Authorization, purpose, and retention are scenario controls.
details.scenarioApplication: Capture only the approved sample in restricted storage with named access, use it for the bounded reproduction, delete it on the agreed schedule, and keep routine logs redacted.
details.transfer: Escalate sensitive diagnostics only through an authorized, purpose-limited capture with controlled access and deletion, while routine telemetry remains redacted.

messages.text: Routine incident logs would expose sensitive prompts and heap material beyond the authorized bounded purpose.
The scenario supplies explicit authorization and controls because lower-sensitivity evidence is already insufficient; postponing the sample leaves the known reproduction gap unresolved.
Indefinite unrestricted collection violates purpose limitation and the recorded access and deletion boundary.
Without restricted storage, named access, and a deletion boundary, the capture is not a controlled exception to the redacted default.
Without bounded use, deletion, and redacted routine telemetry, the sensitive sample can persist or spread beyond the incident.

feedback.reason: Detailed diagnostics are justified only as a bounded, explicitly authorized exception after redacted evidence is insufficient; storage, access, purpose, deletion, and redacted defaults keep the exposure controlled.

options.text: Capture only the authorized diagnostic sample in restricted storage, with named operator access and the recorded deletion date.
Use the sample for the bounded reproduction, delete it under the agreed retention rule, and keep routine telemetry redacted.
Add full prompts and heap data to normal incident logs so support can correlate future cases.
Continue with metadata-only telemetry and revisit the authorized sample if the next reproduction remains inconclusive.
Collect an unrestricted sample indefinitely so later incidents can reuse it without another approval.

questions.prompt: Metadata and redacted timing are insufficient to reproduce a high-memory incident. The organization has explicitly authorized a private diagnostic sample with a named operator, restricted storage, and deletion date; support does not need routine prompt retention. Select TWO actions.

constraints: The provider response and transport status are valid.
The consumer schema version and parser error are available.
The failure occurs at the downstream contract boundary.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the provider response were invalid or an HTTP error reached CI before parsing, provider error classification and request correlation would be the relevant diagnostic branch.
details.errorCorrection: Provider retries, model changes, and timeouts cannot repair a consumer that rejects a valid response; accepting both schemas without versioning moves the failure downstream.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends claude -p for CI and scripts, structured output for programmatic processing, and restricted tools when running unattended. Versioning the consumer contract and adding a test are scenario controls.
details.scenarioApplication: Compare the producer and consumer schema versions, update or roll back the consumer through its change process, add a structured-output contract test, and rerun CI.
details.transfer: When transport and provider output are valid but a consumer rejects the schema, repair and test the versioned interface at the producer-consumer boundary.

messages.text: Availability is normal and the response is valid, so provider retries or model changes do not repair the older consumer contract.
A permissive unversioned parser hides incompatible fields and leaves downstream behavior undefined instead of establishing an accepted schema.
Timeouts and repeated valid responses cannot resolve a schema-version mismatch in the CI consumer.

feedback.reason: A valid provider response does not satisfy an older downstream schema; the producer-consumer contract must be compared and versioned before provider availability is investigated.

options.text: Retry provider calls, switch model if needed, preserve the unchanged consumer schema, and inspect availability again before changing the parser.
Version the producer and consumer contract, update or roll back the consumer through change control, add a structured-output contract test, and rerun CI.
Allow either schema in the consumer parser, keep the interface unversioned, record compatibility as a warning, and let downstream jobs discover incompatible fields.
Increase timeout, repeat calls, compare normal availability, and wait for a later provider response instead of examining the consumer’s schema error.

questions.prompt: The provider returns a response that passes the requested structured-output schema, but the CI consumer rejects it because the consumer still expects an older field version. Request latency and provider availability are normal. What should be repaired first?

constraints: The native-versus-JavaScript memory classification is available.
The JavaScript heap is within its normal range.
Lower-sensitivity runtime and repository evidence can be collected first.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If JavaScript heap usage dominated and remained high after safe-mode and clean-session checks, a private heap snapshot could be appropriate under the documented sensitive-data handling.
details.errorCorrection: A detailed JavaScript artifact does not explain native allocations, while model changes or routine heap capture change or broaden the investigation without addressing the measured resource class.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic's troubleshooting guidance says to try safe mode first, distinguish JavaScript-heap from native-memory pressure, and handle any heap snapshot as sensitive diagnostic data. The native investigation order is scenario policy.
details.scenarioApplication: Preserve the classification, inspect the native-memory path and bounded repository/runtime reproduction, and reserve a restricted JavaScript heap snapshot for a case with measured JavaScript heap growth.
details.transfer: Choose diagnostics by measured resource class; reserve sensitive, detailed artifacts for the class they can actually explain.

messages.text: A JavaScript heap snapshot targets the normal heap, not the measured native allocations, and it creates sensitive data without a matched diagnostic question.
Changing the model or heap allocation does not identify whether native or JavaScript memory causes the incident and can obscure the bounded reproduction.
Discarding the available memory classification and collecting routine heap data broadens sensitive capture while ignoring the native evidence.

feedback.reason: The measured memory class makes an ordinary JavaScript heap snapshot low-yield; native-memory evidence directs the next investigation to runtime or repository loading while sensitive capture remains conditional.

options.text: Take a full JavaScript heap snapshot immediately because the detailed artifact is most informative, then change the model if memory remains.
Preserve the native-versus-JavaScript classification, investigate native/runtime or repository load, and reserve a private JavaScript snapshot for measured JS-heap growth.
Switch model or increase heap allocation before identifying whether native or JavaScript memory accounts for the pressure.
Repeat safe-mode runs without recording memory class, then capture routine heap data for every incident to compare later.

questions.prompt: A bounded reproduction still shows high memory after safe mode and a clean session. Diagnostics indicate native allocations dominate while the JavaScript heap remains within its normal range; the team proposes taking a JavaScript heap snapshot first. What is the best next diagnostic?

constraints: Project-root files, relative command paths, and active configuration sources are inspectable.
The existing setup can be examined without resetting it.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If both directories loaded identical configuration and logs identified an authentication failure, credential repair would become the appropriate next step.
details.errorCorrection: Moving configuration can conceal a project-root defect, while credential refresh and reinstall change components shared by both sessions without first explaining the directory difference.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends /mcp for connection and approval status, targeted MCP debug logging, and checking project paths and relative commands when servers fail.
details.scenarioApplication: Confirm which project configuration is loaded in each directory, inspect the server’s approval and connection status, check relative commands, and enable narrowly targeted diagnostics if necessary.
details.transfer: Use the smallest observed environment difference to choose the first diagnostic comparison.

messages.text: User scope might mask the symptom while broadening the integration to unrelated projects; it does not establish why the project setup differs.
The shared account works in the other directory, so refresh is a weaker first hypothesis than the configuration and approval differences that can be inspected.
A clean executable can help an installation fault, but the same installed version already works in one directory; inspect that contrast before resetting it.

feedback.reason: The directory-dependent behavior is evidence about project discovery, paths, or local approval state. Inspecting those differences is more informative than changing the scope or resetting a shared installation.

options.text: Promote the MCP server and hook to user scope so both directories inherit one shared configuration, then verify the connection.
Refresh the account’s authentication and reconnect the server in both directories before inspecting project configuration differences.
Compare project roots and loaded sources, inspect /mcp approvals and connection status, and use targeted logs for path or command failures.
Reinstall the current CLI version and retest both directories to establish a clean executable before investigating repository-specific settings.

questions.prompt: A project MCP server appears in Claude Code from one repository directory but is missing from another. A project hook also fails to run in the second directory. Both sessions use the same account and installed version. What should the developer inspect first?

constraints: Request IDs, error types, and attempt counts can be retained.
Repository owners can correct invalid configuration.
Retries must be bounded and failures remain visible.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A documented transient condition may justify a retry even when the request is unchanged; an invalid-request response requires correction before another equivalent attempt.
details.errorCorrection: Universal retry, runner restart, and reduced concurrency can help transient conditions but do not change invalid request configuration.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic documents distinct error types, retry-after semantics, exponential backoff for transient failures, and a separate spend-cap condition that keeps failing until access resumes.
details.scenarioApplication: Record the error type and request ID, apply documented backoff to eligible transient failures, and terminate malformed requests visibly with enough context for the owning repository to repair them.
details.transfer: Choose recovery from the failure class and changed preconditions, not merely from a nonzero exit status.

messages.text: A bounded loop is better than an unlimited loop, but replaying a known malformed request still wastes attempts and delays the actionable failure.
A clean process does not repair a configuration value that is sent unchanged in every request.
Lower parallelism addresses congestion, whereas the invalid-request class is caused by request configuration rather than load.

feedback.reason: The payloads already distinguish recoverable service conditions from a deterministic request defect. Recovery should use that evidence instead of making every failure consume the same retry budget.

options.text: Classify the errors, retain request evidence, back off eligible transient failures, and report invalid configuration to its owner without replaying it unchanged.
Apply bounded exponential backoff to every nonzero exit, then assign the final exhausted attempt to the repository owner for classification.
Restart the CI runner after each failed attempt and rerun with the same inputs, using a clean process as the recovery boundary for both error classes.
Reduce parallelism for all failed jobs and requeue them after the congestion window, then compare success rates before changing the request configuration.

questions.prompt: An unattended Claude Code CI job retries every nonzero exit identically. Its structured error payloads show both transient overload responses and invalid-request failures caused by repository configuration. Which recovery design should replace the current policy?
